passages.text: Characterization of treatment intensified (add-on to metformin) adults with type 2 diabetes in Thailand: A cross-sectional real-world study (CONVERGE)
ABSTRACT
Objective

The CONVERGE (Cardiovascular Outcomes and Value in the Real-World with GLP-1RAs) study characterized demographics, clinical characteristics, and medication use in treatment-intensified (add-on to metformin) adults with type 2 diabetes (T2D) in Thailand.
Methods

A retrospective cross-sectional study of data from medical records (Jul 26, 2013, to Dec 31, 2017) was descriptively summarized for overall population and subgroups defined by glucose-lowering agent (GLA) classes.
Results

Data from 1,000 adults were collected in reverse chronological order. At baseline, the mean (SD) age was 60 (12) years, HbA1c was 8.0%, and the median (IQR) T2D duration was 1.0 (0.2-2.4) years. Patients taking SGLT2-is (sodium glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors) had a longer T2D duration (1.8 years, 0.8-3.2), GLP-1RAs (glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists) had a higher body mass index of 32.0 (8.84) kg/m2, and insulin subgroup had a higher HbA1c 8.5% (7.5-10.1). The utilization of GLP-1 RAs/SGLT-2is was low (1.5% and 6%, respectively). Among the subgroups, most patients in the GLP-1RA (80.0%) and insulin subgroup (81.3%) receiving 3/>=4 GLAs. The most frequently prescribed GLAs post-metformin were sulfonylureas (45.2%) and dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (39.4%). Overall, 90% received >=1 cardiovascular (CV) medication; lipid-lowering agents (78%) were the most prescribed.
Conclusions

These results indicate low utilization of GLAs with CV benefits, attributed to a lack of CV benefit data during the study period and partial reimbursement implementation. Future studies must identify barriers to adoption and estimate the usage of these GLAs with CV benefits as more evidence becomes available on positive CV outcomes to improve patient care in Thailand.

The CONVERGE study retrospectively analyzed data from medical records of 1,000 adults with type 2 diabetes in Thailand from 2013 to 2017. The study provided insights into demographics, clinical characteristics, and treatment patterns. Findings indicated suboptimal utilization of cardioprotective glucose-lowering agents such as GLP-1RAs and SGLT-2is, underscoring the need for further research post availability of evidence on positive cardiovascular outcomes to improve patient care in Thailand.
INTRODUCTION

Type 2 diabetes (T2D), characterized by chronic hyperglycemia, is becoming increasingly prevalent in Thailand. In 2021, approximately 6 million adults, or 11.6% of the population, were diagnosed with T2D, positioning Thailand as the country with the fourth-highest incidence in the Western Pacific region. This rising trend is concerning, particularly due to the high prevalence of cardiovascular (CV) complications associated with T2D. Notably, one in three adults with T2D has established cardiovascular disease (CVD). Individuals with T2D experience higher rates of major adverse CV events than those without diabetes. A multicenter study conducted across five tertiary care hospitals in Thailand estimated that about 20% of people with T2D had CVD.

The American Diabetes Association (ADA) and the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) guidelines recommend initiating treatment with metformin monotherapy. If glycemic control remains inadequate after 3 months, the guidelines suggest intensification with additional glucose-lowering agents (GLAs). For patients at risk of CVD or heart failure, medications with cardioprotective effects should be considered as add-ons. Additionally, in people with T2D living with overweight or obesity, the impact of GLAs on weight must be taken into account.

In recent years, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT-2is) have shown significant CV benefits in people with T2D and established CVD or those at risk of CV events. However, the adoption of these newer therapies in clinical practice remains suboptimal. The international CAPTURE study revealed that only two in 10 people with T2D and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease were receiving GLP-1RAs or SGLT-2is.

Evidence supporting the use of newer therapies, such as GLP-1RAs and SGLT-2is, comes mainly from registry studies with stringent inclusion criteria or targeted real-world analyses. The discrepancy between randomized controlled trial settings and routine clinical practice underscores the need for robust real-world evidence to fully understand treatment patterns, particularly in relation to CV parameters in people with T2D. Data characterizing people with T2D with respect to CV-related parameters in the Asia Pacific, including Thailand, remain limited.

The CONVERGE (Cardiovascular Outcomes and Value in the Real-World with GLP-1RAs) study aimed to address this knowledge gap by providing comprehensive data on demographics, clinical characteristics, treatment patterns, and healthcare resource utilization (HCRU) in treatment-intensified T2D adults (those on add-on therapy to metformin) in real-world settings in Thailand.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Study design

This is a cross-sectional analysis utilizing data extracted from medical records. The cohort comprises people diagnosed with T2D, after the first local marketing authorization of GLP-1RAs (exenatide was withdrawn in Apr 2013 and liraglutide was formally launched in 2012), who had undergone treatment intensification post-metformin therapy. To account for the delay between launch and true access to liraglutide, the study period spanned from Jul 26, 2013, to Dec 31, 2017. The first SGLT-2i, dapagliflozin, was launched in Thailand in 2014. The baseline was defined as the date of the first prescription for the most recent GLA class. Specific information from medical records before the baseline was collected, covering intervals of 6 or 12 months (Figure 1).

CONVERGE study design. Date of first prescription for the most recent antidiabetic agent (post-metformin): aOn or after the date of local marketing authorization for the first GLP-1RA at participating treatment centers. bExcluding smoking history. BMI, body mass index; CVD, cardiovascular disease; GLP-1RA, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist; HCRU, healthcare resource utilization.

The primary objective was to characterize demographics, clinical characteristics, medication use, and HCRU among eligible Thai people with T2D who were prescribed additional GLAs as an add-on to metformin. The secondary objectives included characterizing the demographics, clinical characteristics, and HCRU in subgroups of patients defined by GLA class post-metformin. These included sulfonylureas (SUs), dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (DPP-4is), GLP-1RAs, SGLT-2is, insulins, and others (not limited to thiazolidinedione, meglitinide, acarbose, biguanide either as monotherapy or in combinations).
Study participants, settings, location

The study analyzed medical records of adults (aged 18-70 years) with a documented T2D diagnosis post-availability of GLP-1RAs in Thailand. Other inclusion criteria included medical records documenting previous or ongoing treatment with metformin and other GLAs. People with diagnosis of type 1 diabetes were excluded from the study.

Due to the study's descriptive design, a formal sample size calculation was not performed. Based on feasibility rather than hypothesis testing, the actual number of eligible patients included in Thailand is 1,000. Recruitment followed a reverse chronological approach since the pool of eligible patients exceeded 1,000.

Data collection involved reviewing medical records from a single tertiary care institution in Thailand. An existing T2D electronic dataset, extracted directly from hospital electronic medical records (EMRs) covering patient interactions across various hospital care settings (e.g., in-patient, out-patient, and emergency department), laboratory tests, and prescription databases was utilized. Authorized personnel at the site linked the existing T2D electronic dataset with the hospital's EMR using patient identifiers.
Study measures

Demographic information, including age, sex, ethnicity, and the date and details of the most recently prescribed GLAs, was collected at baseline. Height, weight (kg), body mass index (BMI) [kg/m2], and clinical parameters [fasting plasma glucose (FPG; mg/dL), glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c; %), total cholesterol (TC; mg/dL), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL; mg/dL), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL; mg/dL), blood pressure (mm/Hg), high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP; mg/L)] were recorded at baseline or within 6 months before baseline. Prescription details, including the date and the total number of CVD drug classes, in addition to the number of T2D- and CVD-related concomitant medication classes, were collected within 12 months before baseline.

Health data from the inception of medical records included T2D diagnosis date, T2D duration, smoking history, the earliest prescription date of metformin, the number of previously prescribed glucose-lowering drug classes, any prescription of CVD medications, diagnosis of CVD and cerebrovascular (CVA) events, existing comorbidities, T2D-related complications. Information related to T2D and CVD management and the relationship to HCRU, including the number of consultations, emergency room (ER) visits, hospitalizations, length of hospital stay (LOS; days), and the number of T2D and CVD-related laboratory tests, was collected since the start of medical records.
Statistical analysis

All eligible adults with T2D constituted the full analysis set (FAS). These data were descriptively summarized, and analyses were carried out for the FAS and subgroups defined by the specific glucose-lowering treatment received at baseline. The CV risk among people with T2D was assessed using the risk engine model from the UK Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS) that predicts the risk of coronary heart disease (CHD) in people with T2D. All HCRU variables were normalized to a per patient per year (PPPY) rate. The PPPY rate was determined by dividing the total number of days of HCRU from T2D diagnosis to the baseline by the number of years since the diagnosis. The LOS analysis was conducted in the subgroup of patients with at least one hospitalization. All analyses were conducted using R [version >=4.1.0, R Core Team (2017) Vienna, Austria].
RESULTS

Initially, 55,333 patients were identified from the electronic data source, characterized by a diagnosis of T2D who were prescribed GLAs. After applying full inclusion/exclusion criteria, 5,850 patients (10.6%) were eligible. A sample of 1,000 patients was included for the full analysis employing reverse chronological order (Figure 2).
Patient disposition. T2D, type 2 diabetes.
Baseline and clinical characteristics

Table 1 presents the baseline demographics and clinical characteristics of the included participants. The mean [standard deviation (SD)] age of the participants was 60.1 (12.07) years, with the lowest mean age in the GLP-1RA subgroup (54.0 [12.55] years), followed by the SGLT-2i subgroup, 57.5 (11.88) years. Male and female participants were equally represented, but female participants were predominant in the GLP-1RA and SGLT-2i subgroups (66.7% and 55.0%, respectively). The median (interquartile range [IQR]) duration from T2D diagnosis to baseline was 1.0 year (0.2-2.4). Patients in the SGLT-2i subgroup had the longest duration of diabetes (1.8 years, 0.8-3.2), followed by the GLP-1 RAs (1.6 years, 0.4-2.6), insulin (1.5 years, 0.6-2.7), DPP-4i (1.0 years, 0.2-2.3), others (0.9 years, 0.2-2.3), and SU (0.8 years, 0.1-2.2) subgroups. The median FPG and HbA1c at baseline were 145.0 mg/dL (117-190) and 7.7% (6.6-9.0), respectively; majority of patients had HbA1c >= 7.0% (65.4%). The insulin subgroup had the highest median HbA1c at 8.5% (7.5-10.1%). The mean BMI was 27.1 (5.78) kg/m2, highest in the GLP1-RA subgroup, 32.0 (8.84) kg/m2. A considerable proportion of participants were living with overweight (36.7%) or obesity (24.6%).

Glucose-lowering treatment characteristics

Metformin was the most commonly prescribed GLA (81.3%), followed by SUs (45.2%) and DPP-4is (39.4%). The incidence of prescriptions for SGLT-2is (6.0%) and GLP-1RAs (1.5%) was low (Figure 3a). Before baseline, most patients were treated with two or more classes of GLAs (70.8%). The insulin (81.3%), GLP-1RA (80.0%), and SGLT-2i (65.0%) subgroups reported the highest proportion of participants receiving three or more classes of GLAs (Figure 3b). Only a small percentage of people with obesity were prescribed GLP-1RAs (8 out of 218). Similarly, limited people with CVD received SGLT-2is (17 out of 207).

A patient could receive multiple glucose-lowering agents at baseline.
CVD treatment characteristics

78.5% of participants received CVD medications since the start of medical records. The SGLT-2i subgroup had the highest proportion of participants receiving CVD medications (95.0%), but they constituted only a fraction of the overall CVD population (7.2%). A total of 497 (49.7%) participants in the FAS had at least 12 months of medical records from T2D diagnosis to baseline; of these, 89.5% received one or more CVD medication classes. Lipid-lowering therapies were the most frequently (77.9%) prescribed CVD drug class, followed by non-angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors/angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) [60.2%], ACE inhibitors/ARBs (47 7%), and anti-platelets (36.0%; Figure 4).

A patient could receive multiple glucose-lowering agents at baseline.
Comorbidities

Overall, 20.7% of the study population were diagnosed with CVD, and 21.6% were identified to be at high CV risk. Ischemic heart disease was reported in 139 (13.9%) patients, CVA disease in 58 (5.8%), heart failure in 38 (3.8%), myocardial infarction in 26 (2.6%) and peripheral vascular diseases in 20 (2.0%) patients. The highest prevalence of CVD was observed within the SGLT-2i (17 of 60, 28.3%) subgroup. More than half of patients were diagnosed with either hypertension (57.8%), dyslipidemia (51.8%), or both, with the highest prevalence observed in the insulin subgroup (66.0% and 61.3%, respectively). In patients with high CV risk (n = 216), 38.5% had LDL >=100 mg/dL, and 52.9% had SBP >=130 mmHg. Diabetes-related complications were reported in 15.0% of patients, with the highest proportion in the insulin (32.7%) and GLP1-RA (26.7%) subgroups.
HCRU

The median [IQR] healthcare professional (HCP) consultations related to T2D were 3.3 (1.1-7.3) PPPY. GLP-1RA and insulin subgroups reported the highest median rates of T2D-related HCP consultations, at 4.1 PPPY and 4.0 PPPY, respectively. The median number of ED visits and hospitalizations due to CVD-related and T2D-related visits was 0 PY. However, this should be interpreted cautiously as it suggests a lack of information regarding ED visits in the database. Among patients with at least one hospitalization, the median LOS for CVD-related and T2D-related hospitalization was 7.1 days [2.5-23.0] and 8.2 days [3.0-27.0] PPPY, respectively. The median number of CVD-related and T2D-related laboratory tests was 9.4 [5.4-18.1] and 9.9 [6.2-16.5] PPPY, respectively. The median number of CVD-related and T2D-related concomitant medication drug classes prescribed within 12 months prior to baseline was 1.1 [0.3-3.3] and 1.4 [0.5-4.3] PPPY, respectively.
DISCUSSION

The current study reports the real-world scenario of T2D management in Thailand, focusing on GLP-1RAs. While demonstrating an underutilization of therapies with established CV benefits, this study also highlights the need for strategies to improve the adoption of newer treatments to better address the high CV risk among people with T2D. The baseline demographics were similar to other local and global real-world studies. Mean age (60.1 years) was consistent with the findings (age: 61.1 years) from a comprehensive Thai survey among 180,000 respondents with diabetes. The mean age was lower in GLP-1RA (54.0 years) and SGLT-2i (57.5 years) subgroups, which is in-line with other studies. A study from Japan found that the risk of hypoglycemia increased by 50% for every 10-year rise in age among patients on SGLT-2is. While GLP-1RAs have not been associated with an elevated hypoglycemia risk in the elderly, the mode of administration may deter their use. Consequently, HCPs often opt for DPP-4is for older patients, given their lower hypoglycemia risk and ease of administration.

In comparison with other studies, our research found a notably short duration from T2D diagnosis to baseline treatment, averaging 1.0 year. The shorter time to baseline treatment likely results from referrals from other healthcare facilities, raising the chance of underestimating the disease duration and comorbidities. The time from diagnosis to treatment varied with patients on SUs beginning treatment within approximately 0.8 years while those on SGLT-2i starting around 1.8 years after diagnosis. This indicates a preference for using conventional diabetes therapies before SGLT-2i, which is often preferred as a later-line treatment option.

Thailand's universal healthcare coverage includes multiple schemes with varied extent of coverage potentially influencing patient outcomes. For instance, patients under the civil servant medical benefit scheme exhibited better glucose control than those under the universal health coverage scheme due to better medication coverage and accessibility. In our study, metformin and SUs were the most common baseline treatments, reflecting both local and global patterns. Despite international guidelines recommending GLP-1RAs and SGLT-2is as second-line therapies post-metformin, their use was low, at 6.0% and 1.5%, respectively. These rates closely match those from the DISCOVER study (SGLT-2is, 4.3% and GLP-1RAs, 1.3%). In lower to middle income countries such as Thailand, the cost often determines medication preference towards more affordable options like SUs before other GLAs. The low utilization of GLAs with CV benefits may also be attributed to the timing of the study period, as positive findings from CV outcome trials for SGLT2is and GLP-1RAs were published in 2015 and 2016, respectively, during the latter half of the data collection period. In addition, only certain schemes in Thailand's healthcare coverage reimburse these GLAs due to their higher costs, particularly the civil servant medical benefit scheme, which covers only 6% of the Thai population. More evidence, including cost-effectiveness, is required for the expansion of GLA access to other coverage schemes. Lastly, awareness and familiarity in primary and secondary care settings are as important in determining a paradigm shift in prescription patterns.

Patients in the insulin, GLP-1RA and SGLT-2i subgroups had the highest numbers of prescribed GLAs across three or more drug classes. A lower proportion of patients received insulin and metformin combination therapy compared to insulin and DPP-4i combination, likely due to the higher perceived risk of hypoglycemia with insulin and metformin combination. However, a recent meta-analysis has shown that the risk of hypoglycemia is increased with insulin and SUs combinations, while insulin combined with other agents, like metformin and DPP-4i, had similar hypoglycemia risks.

Obesity was highly prevalent (24.6%), underscoring the region's growing concern. This prevalence aligns with findings from other studies in Thailand, which reported that approximately 50-60% of people with T2D are categorized as overweight or living with obesity. Guidelines emphasize the importance of weight control for people with T2D as sustained weight loss (>10%) offers disease-modifying effects on glycemia and improves long-term CV outcomes and mortality. Despite the emerging evidence on the weight loss benefits of GLP-1RAs and the cardioprotective benefits of SGLT-2is, a considerable treatment gap remains. The subgroup of patients prescribed GLP-1RAs had the highest proportion of obesity (57.1%), indicating a preference for weight reduction benefits, however, the overall prescription rates still remained very low. It is pertinent to consider the recent availability of GLP-1RAs and SGLT-2i, or lack thereof, which could contribute to low adoption in clinical practice. Future studies could explore potential barriers such as cost and accessibility factors to the low prescription of these agents in at-risk groups.

In this study, 20.7% of patients were diagnosed with CVD, which aligns with findings from a multicenter cross-sectional study in Thailand. This prevalence exceeds the 14.6% reported in the multinational DISCOVER study, suggesting the potential influence of tertiary care settings, which often see more severe T2D individuals with multiple comorbidities, including CVD. Majority had used CVD medications prior to baseline (78.5%), indicating a focus on primary prevention of CVD events. This is consistent with the high prevalence of hypertension (57.8%) and dyslipidemia (51.8%) observed in this study and also aligns with another study in Thailand, which reported approximately half of people with diabetes had either hypertension, elevated LDL, or both. Overall, the management of CVD is in-line with the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines recommending the use of anti-hypertensive, lipid-lowering, and anti-platelet therapy in people with CVD risk factors.

The SGLT-2i subgroup reported the highest burden of CVD (28.3%) and extensive use of CVD medications (95%). This suggests a prescribing pattern aligned with emerging evidence supporting the long-term CVD benefits of SGLT-2is in people with T2D. HbA1c levels were high (mean 8.0%), with most of them having HbA1c >= 7.0%. Similarly, LDL levels and systolic blood pressure was high (mean 106.6 mg/dL; mean 132.4 mmHg). A large Thai study reported similar findings (mean HbA1c of 8.0% and approximately 65% with HbA1c >= 7.0%). Further, 21.6% of the study population were identified as having high CV risk, suggesting the importance of proactive management strategies. However, the CV risk might be underestimated due to missing data for key risk factors: HbA1c, TC, and HDL were missing for 13.8%, 20.9%, and 38.9% of individuals, respectively. These missing variables were assigned reference values, potentially diluting the calculated CV risk.

In this study, 15.0% of the study population reported diabetes-related complications, which was similar to 19.4% reported in the DISCOVER study. The incidence of diabetic retinopathy was 10.9%, comparable to the 13.7% found in another population-based study in Thailand. Patients prescribed insulin had the highest proportion of diabetes-related complications (32.7%). Insulin is typically used in later lines for patients with more severe disease and poor glucose control, as evidenced by a median HbA1c of 8.5% in our cohort. The number of T2D-related HCP visits (median 3.3 PPPY), approximately one visit every 3-4 months, was broadly comparable to another study in Thailand (median 4-5 visits per year). The highest number of T2D-related HCP consultations were observed in the GLP-1RA and insulin subgroups. These patients also reported the highest number of diabetes-related complications (26.7% and 32.7% respectively), indicating a higher T2D disease severity. The number of HCP visits linked to CVD, were low (median 0 PPPY), even though 20% of individuals had CVD and another 20% were considered to be at high CV risk. There had not been any incident CVD events that required HCP visits, considering the one-year median T2D duration. Literature evidence suggests that incident CVD development occurs within 3-4 years.

In addition, our research found that the median number of hospital admissions and ED visits for people with diabetes was lower than in another study conducted in Thailand. This may be attributed to the absence of consolidated patient data among various healthcare institutions, which may result in an underestimation of the number of patients from this study who seek ED care or hospital admission at other healthcare sites. The GLP-1RA subgroup exhibited the shortest CVD-related LOS (median 4.5 days) among individuals who had undergone at least one hospitalization. Although, a shorter CVD-related LOS could be speculated for CV benefits of the GLP-1RA, demonstrated in other studies, but the small sample size undermines this claim. The number of CVD and T2D-related lab tests (about one visit every 1.5 months) was higher than the ADA-recommended timeframe of 3-6 months for HbA1c tests. This may be the result of inadequate glucose (65.4% with HbA1c >= 7.0%) and lipid control (TC levels; 175 mg/dL), requiring routine laboratory monitoring.

This observational study, subject to potential confounding factors, reflected routine clinical practice rather than mandatory assessments at prespecified time points, potentially impacting data frequency and interpretation. However, data extraction from a single tertiary academic hospital's EMRs from an urban setting introduced a risk. Patients from this site may have experienced better care and outcomes compared to those at non-teaching hospitals. Health-seeking behaviors, access to specialist care, and treatment affordability might vary between urban and rural areas, possibly leading to an overrepresentation of recent and expensive T2D treatments in the findings. The inclusion of a single tertiary care hospital indicates an overrepresentation of those with severe disease and these patients are commonly referred from primary care due to suboptimal disease management. However, despite the disease being more severe, HCRU, that is, ED visits and hospitalizations, were low, possibly due to the inability to capture HCRU visits outside of the study site. There was also a risk of ascertainment bias, as diagnoses defined the presence of comorbidities. Excluding proxies, such as procedures, could have underestimated comorbidity prevalence. Finally, there may have been an information bias risk, as diagnoses or treatments prescribed outside the study site were not captured. This could have led to an underestimation of the disease burden and healthcare utilization.

In summary, this study underscored the significant burden of uncontrolled diabetes and notable CVD risk among people with T2D in Thailand. However, the use of newer cardioprotective GLAs such as GLP-1RAs and SGLT-2is remains limited both overall and in at-risk populations. Further research is needed to understand the barriers to adopting these newer agents, which offer additional CV benefits to improve patient outcomes in the context of T2D management in Thailand.

passages.text: "From my life, she will never be gone, even though she is no longer here" - a single case interpretative phenomenological analysis on spousal loss and resilience
ABSTRACT

Older people often face drastic life events, such as spousal loss, that profoundly affect their daily lives. Consequently, resilience:how one navigates life's changes to avoid further adverse outcomes:is increasingly relevant in ageing studies. Although understanding older adults' resilience is key to preventing adverse outcomes, the complexity of loss-related events and everyday resilience in later life is underexplored from a process-based perspective. This study employs an Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA) case study of one individual to investigate resilience in response to spousal loss from a process-based perspective. Four interviews were conducted with this one participant and data was analysed following IPA guidelines. Findings indicate how resilience, in this case, resembles a process of continuous adaptation and renewal or "bouncing forward", in the face of diverse adversities, as written by Bourbeau. This study enriches our understanding of the process-based perspective on resilience, which is essential for concretely defining resilience and its practical application.
Introduction

Spousal loss is recognized by several authors as one of the most stressful life events to occur in one's life (Holmes & Rahe,; Infurna & Luthar,; Yu et al.,). Such loss is prevalent in later life and often entails shattering of a "taken for granted" world (Fang & Carr,). This requires (re)defining meaning of identity and existence after losing a relationship that has likely influenced everyday life and identity (Fang,; Fang & Carr,; Larsson et al.,; Naef et al.,; Richardson,). This major life event is well documented as having several potential injurious outcomes (Stahl & Schulz,) such as intense suffering (Holmes & Rahe,), decline in physical and mental health (Ang,; Buckley et al.,; Jones et al.,; Lee & Carr,; Shear et al.,; Utz et al.,) and higher risk of mortality (Holland et al.,; Manzoli et al.,; van den Berg et al.,). Why injurious outcomes occur and persist in later life for some people but not for others remains a question of wide interest (Beeris et al.,). The concept of resilience is valuable in this regard. It illustrates how people navigate adversities to prevent further adverse outcomes (Amaral et al.,; Browne-Yung et al.,; Hayman et al.,; Wiles et al.,; Wild et al.,; Wiles et al.,; Wilson et al.,).

In research on resilience in later life, emphasis is often placed on resource- and outcome-based perspectives on resilience and a detailed, concrete understanding of resilience from a process-based perspective is lacking (Beeris et al.,; Glas et al.,). Put simply, the helpful components and objectives for resilience in later life are clear; however, understanding of the mechanisms involved in applying them in real-life settings, as well as how one experiences this, remains underdeveloped. Gaining deeper insight into these mechanisms is crucial for accurately defining resilience and informing how resilience operates and is experienced in practice. This knowledge informs appropriate and timely resilience-enhancing practices, potentially preventing further adverse outcomes when navigating life's challenges.

In light of these considerations, this paper aims to develop an understanding of the mechanisms that facilitate different outcomes when navigating adversity and how these mechanisms are experienced. To achieve this, an IPA case study of one individual is utilized to examine the interaction of adversity, outcomes, and the underlying mechanisms involved in navigating the highly disruptive and prevalent life event of spousal loss. Specifically, this paper seeks to answer the following research question: How does one experience navigating the adversities associated with spousal loss to prevent the occurrence and persistence of further injurious outcomes?
Theoretical framework
Spousal loss

In this paper, we identify spousal loss to involve two distinct phenomena: bereavement and widowhood. According to Bennett and Soulsby on one hand, bereavement regards the state of having experienced the death of one's spouse and the personal consequences and meanings this brings. Widowhood on the other hand, is a long-term state that does not only carry personal consequences but also carries long-term social consequences and meanings such as changes in friendships, social support, and changes in status within society. One can experience high levels of resilience in bereavement for example, and struggle with doing so in widowhood (Bennett,).

The grieving process experienced during spousal loss is also widely written about. Freud largely influenced early theories on grief with his paper on Mourning and Melancholia (Ang,; Hall,). He recommended for example the severing of energetic ties with the deceased in order to be able to move forward. Following Freud, stage theories became popular, structuring grief into a series of stages and tasks (Ang,; Hall,), the most well-known being from Kubler-Ross. Several authors, however, emphasize that while stage theories offer valuable insights, they fail to fully capture the complexity and idiosyncratic nature of the grieving experience (Ang,; Hall,; Stroebe & Schut,; Worden,). Furthermore, Klass et al. emphasize the concept of "continued bonds," asserting that death does not signify the end of a relationship. They highlight a potentially beneficial role of maintaining these bonds, even though the other has passed away. Two of the most widely influential contemporary models of grief seek to capture the complexity of both the grieving process and continued bonds (Hall,), namely the Dual Process Model of Grief (Stroebe & Schut,) and the Task-Based Model (Worden,).
Resilience

Resilience is challenging to define and lacks a standardized definition (Angevaare et al.,). Nonetheless, consensus is strengthening that an operable definition of resilience should incorporate three elements: adversity, outcome, and mechanisms (Angevaare et al.,; IJntema et al.,; Van Breda,). Firstly, adversity can be defined as "particular (often extraordinary) embodied and emplaced circumstances in people's lives that cause pain, disruption, exhaustion, disorientation, loneliness, and grief" (Power et al.,, p. 2). Adversity is also referred to in literature on resilience in later life as a stressor, challenge, risk, unfavourable condition or threat (Angevaare et al.,). Secondly, outcome refers to developments that unfold as a consequence of facing adversity. See for example, the psychological immunity-psychological elasticity (PI-PE) model which illustrates adaption to adversity through thriving, sustainability, recovery or transformation, or maladaptation through rigidity and vulnerability (IJntema et al.,). Finally, the third essential element, mechanisms, are the interactions that facilitate varying outcomes when navigating adversity (Angevaare et al.,). These interactions occur within and between several levels, that is, individual, community and society and incorporate engagement of essential factors or resources.

Different perspectives can be utilized to deepen understanding of how resilience works when facing challenging life events, such as spousal loss; namely, resource-based, outcome-based, and process-based perspectives (Beeris et al.,). Firstly, resource-based perspectives focus on the essential factors or resources of individuals or groups identified as being "resilient", for example physical, mental and cognitive health, living conditions and social support (Angevaare et al.,). These resources and factors are identified across multiple levels:individual, community, and societal:demonstrating that resilience extends beyond personal traits or capacities to include broader contextual and relational dimensions. Secondly, outcome-based perspectives focus on the outcomes that unfold when an individual or a group of people is faced with adversity. What authors consider to be a "resilient outcome" however varies significantly (Angevaare et al.,; Beeris et al.,). As highlighted by Luthar and Brown resilience is never an "across the board" phenomenon. There are a range of outcomes, from more negative to more positive (Condly,). Thirdly, process-based perspectives focus on the mechanisms involved in navigating adversity and facilitating varying outcomes, emphasizing that these mechanisms manifest dynamically depending on timing and context throughout one's life course (Beeris et al.,; Glas et al.,; Voie et al.,). See, for example, how Bourbeau describes resilience as a process of "bouncing forward." This process of "bouncing forward" conceptualizes how individuals navigate the dynamic, ever-shifting, and context-dependent interaction of adversity and outcomes across one's lifespan. Rather than "bouncing back" to a pre-adversity state or progressing towards static and fixed outcomes, this interaction fosters continuous adaptation and renewal.
Research design and methods
Research design

This paper employs a case study of one individual in combination with Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA) which is a technique endorsed by Smith et al.. This is, nevertheless, quite distinctive as "the balance between case studies and studies using larger sample sizes is currently biased in favour of the latter, to the extent that it disadvantages case studies in most disciplines" (Flyvbjerg,, p. 242). Single-case studies have been widely and often mistakenly critiqued for being highly subjective, slow, costly, and of low scientific value (Flyvbjerg,; Stake,). The decision to use this method was therefore carefully deliberated, as recommended by Stake, and the choice to pursue it was driven by the following reasons.

Firstly, single-case studies are often used to explore complex issues with limited prior research and to promote a holistic understanding of a phenomenon (Flyvbjerg,; Kumar,; Stake,; Verschuren,), making this approach well-suited to this paper's research aim. To develop a process-based understanding of resilience, a method capable of capturing depth and richness was required:something uniquely offered by the single-case study (Westers & Peters,). Furthermore, by employing this approach, this study could conduct a deep, detailed exploration of an individual experience, maximizing what could be learned from a single case while critically reflecting on broader generalizations and future research directions in resilience. That is to say, despite the emphasis on particularization, this paper's case study is an "instrumental case study" (Stake,, p. 3). It focuses on the particular in order to reflect upon issues extending beyond the case itself, aligning seamlessly with this paper's aim.

The unique combination with IPA also strengthened the choice for a single-case study approach. While case studies are often characterized by open-ended techniques of data collection and analysis (Kumar,), IPA provides concrete guidelines for gathering and interpreting qualitative data (Smith et al.,). Moreover, IPA explicitly focuses specifically on individuals' interpretations of their experiences and is particularly concerned with instances when everyday experiences take on significant meaning, typically following major life events (Smith et al.,). As such, it offers appropriate tools for this paper to obtain a rich account of how one experiences navigating adversities associated with spousal loss. Additionally, Stake explains how when using a case study, the researcher has an ethical obligation to minimize misinterpretation and misunderstanding of the case study. IPA provides a solid framework to guide this process, strengthening integrity and robustness substantially.

Our choice for an IPA case study of one individual was therefore driven by our research aim. The single IPA case study offered the tools to best approach the task at hand. The emphasis on a single case study in this research should therefore not be regarded as a dismissal of studies that utilize larger samples or populations. Rather, it is intended to be complementary. While larger samples offer significant advantages in terms of breadth, they often suffer from a lack of depth. Conversely, case studies provide in-depth insights but lack breadth. Therefore, both approaches are essential for optimal, well-balanced and comprehensive development of research (Flyvbjerg,; Verschuren,).
Participant selection

This paper is part of a larger, ongoing research project conducted in collaboration with social welfare and healthcare organizations in three Dutch municipalities. Professionals from these partner organizations acted as gatekeepers in the search for eligible participants.

Case studies and IPA conventionally work with purposively selected participants who can provide insight into a specific perspective on a phenomenon (Flyvbjerg,; Smith et al.,; Stake,). We therefore purposively sought participants aged 65 or older, comprising two men and two women, all residing in the same area of the Netherlands, whose long-term perspective on spousal loss could offer insights into the process of resilience over time. Further inclusion criteria required participants to have directly experienced spousal loss at least one year prior to the interview and to retain an active memory of the event. Exclusion criteria included mental health issues or physical limitations at the time of recruitment that would hinder safe participation.

One of the four participants found, Bas (pseudonym), was selected as the case study for this paper. The absence of a maximum time frame for partner loss made Bas's case unique and valuable to analyse as a single-case study. Bas, a 76-year-old Dutch male, lost his wife, Elly (also a pseudonym), 30 years before the interviews. His experience, spanning three decades, provided a detailed account of changes in navigating adversity and resilience from bereavement into widowhood.

Before any interview took place with Bas, he was informed about the research project and privacy protocol in an initial briefing. Bas was also provided with a formal invitation letter, which outlined the project's overarching aim, what he could expect from the interview, and data management. The letter also informed him that he could withdraw from the research at any time without providing a reason, and that all data from his interviews would be deleted or destroyed upon withdrawal. Bas was given "thinking time" after this meeting. Once he agreed to participate, he signed informed consent forms and only after this point did the interviews begin.
Data gathering

Bas was interviewed four times in semi-structured interviews following the IPA guidelines by Smith et al.. It was estimated that four interviews would be needed to allow for a gradual pace and to build rapport between Bas and the researcher. This was deemed necessary given the emotional nature of his story. Bas chose a location for the interviews where he felt comfortable and where interruptions were minimal: his own home. A topic list with suggested questions and probes was used to structure the interviews. All interviews were recorded with an audio recorder and ranged in duration from 55 min to 69 min. The audio files were uploaded to a secure drive at the University of Humanistic Studies in Utrecht, the Netherlands, immediately after the interviews and then deleted from the recorder. In between each interview, the interviewer would listen to the audio recording of the previous interview. Adjustments were made to the topic list questions and probes where additional information or clarification was needed. This process, from recruiting to completing the interviews, took place over 5 months.
Data analysis

After the interviews took place, they were transcribed verbatim as required for IPA. These transcripts were also uploaded to the same secure drive as the audio files. The transcripts were then anonymized and analysed following IPA guidelines (Smith et al.,). Analysis therefore followed an iterative and inductive cycle, ensuring findings are firmly rooted in the interview data and that new information and perspectives were accommodated as the analysis progressed. This process involved what is called a double hermeneutic as the analyst tries to make sense of how a participant is making sense of what has happened to them. Analysis therefore began with careful reading and re-reading the interviews. This was followed by line-by-line engagement with the transcripts, where extensive notes were written on the descriptive, linguistic and conceptual aspects of the participant narratives. From these notes, experiential statements were constructed. They are "experiential" as they relate directly to the participants' experiences and "statements" as they are constructed into statement form. This step concisely summarizes chunks of texts and extensive notes into statements, breaking up the narrative flow of the interviews.

The following step involved identification of emerging themes amongst the experiential statements. These are called Personal Experiential Themes (PET's). To form PET's, included experiential statements were clustered in terms of alignment with one another, altering the chronological order of the statements. Each cluster was given a title to describe its characteristics and hereby became a PET. Under each PET, experiential statements were divided further into sub-themes.
Rigor & presentation of data

Making sense of the data requires a strict interpretative engagement on part of the researcher with a high level of reflexivity (Smith et al.,). To strengthen validity, extensive meetings took place between all authors to discuss all interpretations and decisions made. Any disagreements were discussed and together plans were made to adjust the analysis accordingly. The same approach was taken in the writing of this article.

Furthermore, criteria for reporting qualitative research (Jars-Qual), published by Levitt et al. were closely followed, as recommended by Smith et al.. This provides guidelines on writing up qualitative research that can be operationalized well in IPA, enabling the reader to make an accurate estimate of its validity. Criteria included are, for example, clear focus on experience and/or participants sense-making, clear account of the purposive sampling in participant selection, clear indication of degree of structure in data collection, an account of how PET's and subthemes were generated, an assessment and comment upon adequacy of data in terms of research question and presentation of findings in figures, tables and dialogue with data.
Findings
PETs and sub-themes.
