Patterns of codon usage in the mitochondrial genome of N. hainanensis.
RSCU of PCGs in the mitochondrial genome of N. hainanensis. The X-axis shows the codons, and the Y-axis shows RSCU values.

RSCU analysis reveals distinct codon frequency biases. Specific codons, including ACT, UCA, UUA, and CGA, exhibit notably higher usage frequencies (Fig. 3). All codons are used a total of 3631 times (Table 3). Codons encoding Phe, Ile, and Met are highly represented, each exceeding 300 occurrences, whereas the Cys codon is the least frequent, appearing only 51 times (Fig. 2; Table 3) (Supplementary file 1). All AA demonstrate preferential utilization of codons with A/U in the third position, such as UAU for Tyr, GUU for Val, and CAA for Gln (Table 3). Among PCGs, Met constitutes the highest proportion (8.9%), while Cys is the least abundant (1.4%) (Fig. 3). These findings indicate pronounced AA bias in the PCGs of N. hainanensis.
The Ka, Ks, and Ka/Ks values of the 13 mitochondrial PCGs in Aradidae.

In terms of evolutionary rates, the evolutionary rates of the 13 PCGs vary, but the Ka/Ks values are all less than 1 (Fig. 4) (Supplementary file 2). Among these, atp8 (Ka/Ks = 0.65), nad2 (0.49), and nad6 (0.48) exhibit the highest evolutionary rates, suggesting potential roles in Aradidae evolution. In contrast, cox1 displays the lowest rate (0.09), followed by cob (0.11) and cox3 (0.12) (Fig. 4).
tRNAs, rRNAs and control region
The putative tRNA secondary structures of N. hainanensis mitochondrial genome.

The mitochondrial genome of N. hainanensis contains 22 tRNA genes ranging from 61 to 69 bp in length, with a total length of 1432 bp. trnA is the shortest at 61 bp, while trnQ, trnS2, and trnV are the longest at 69 bp (Table 1). Fourteen tRNAs are encoded on the J-strand, and eight on the N-strand (Fig. 1; Table 1). The tRNA genes exhibit an A + T content of 71.2%, with positive AT-skew and GC-skew (Table 2). Most tRNAs form complete cloverleaf structures; however, trnS1 lacks the DHU arm, preventing formation of the typical structure. The tRNA secondary structures contain 32 base mismatches in addition to the normal base pairs, including examples such as trnF (U-G) and trnG (U-G, A-A). Mismatched pairs comprise U-G (30 times) and A-A (2 times) (Fig. 5).

The rrnL gene is 1255 bp in length, and the rrnS gene is 743 bp, both located on the N-strand (Fig. 1). Both genes exhibit negative AT-skew and positive GC-skew (Table 2). A control region of 817 bp is positioned between the rrnS and trnQ (Fig. 1), with a nucleotide composition of A (34.4%), T (31.1%), C (17.6%), and G (16.9%) (Table 2).
Heterogeneity analysis
Heterogeneity analysis based on PCG12, PCG123, and AA datasets. The deeper the color of the blue square, the lower the heterogeneity. Conversely, the higher the heterogeneity.

The figure indicates the heterogeneity of nucleotide differences (Fig. 6). All three datasets (AA, PCG12, and PCG123) exhibit low heterogeneity levels, supporting their suitability for phylogenetic reconstruction. The greatest divergence in heterogeneity is observed between the AA and PCG123 datasets, with AA displaying the lowest heterogeneity and PCG123 the highest. The PCG12 dataset (excluding third codon positions) demonstrates reduced heterogeneity compared to PCG123, indicating that the third codon position has a high heterogeneity rate (Fig. 6).
Phylogenetic relationships

The BI tree of Pentatomomorpha based on dataset PCG12. Numbers at the nodes are posterior probabilities. Different color blocks represent the various superfamilies within Pentatomomorpha. Different colored dots represent the various subfamilies within Aradidae.

The ML tree of Pentatomomorpha based on dataset PCG12. Numbers at the nodes are bootstrap values. Different color blocks represent the various superfamilies within Pentatomomorpha. Different colored dots represent the various subfamilies within Aradidae.

The phylogenetic trees reconstructed by BI and ML methods exhibit nearly identical topologies, with all nodes demonstrating high support values. The inferred relationships within Pentatomomorpha are reconstructed as (Aradoidea + (Pentatomoidea + (Lygaeoidea + (Coreoidea + Pyrrhocoroidea)))) (Figs. 7 and 8) (Supplementary file 3-6). Aradoidea is strongly supported as monophyletic and occupies a stable taxonomic position, consistently placed at the base of Pentatomomorpha. The remaining superfamilies form two primary clades: one comprising the monophyletic Pentatomoidea, and the other consisting of paraphyletic Pyrrhocoroidea, Coreoidea, and Lygaeoidea, with all critical nodes exhibiting high support values.

N. hainanensis belongs to Neuroctenus, and the phylogeny supports Neuroctenus as a monophyletic group. The four Neuroctenus species cluster into a single lineage, forming a sister group to Mezira sp. Additionally, Aradacanthia is positioned at the base of Aradidae, indicating that Aradacanthia heissi represents an early-diverging lineage (Figs. 7 and 8).
Discussion

The mitochondrial genome sequence of N. hainanensis is 15,213 bp, representing a typical closed double-stranded circular DNA molecule. It comprises 37 genes and a control region, consistent with the characteristics of a standard insect mitochondrial genome. Both the entire mitochondrial genome and PCGs exhibit a high A + T content, showing a distinct AT bias, which aligns with observations in other Aradidae species. The bias in base composition is widely attributed to two key factors: asymmetric mutation of the four bases and selective pressure, both primarily arising from replication and gene transcription processes.

Codon usage analysis reveals that Aradidae species preferentially employ ATN as start codons, with TAA or TAG being the predominant termination codons. The codon usage pattern of N. hainanensis aligns closely with other Aradidae species. cox1, cox2, and nad1 use TTG as their start codon, which not only reduces the intergenic space but also prevents adjacent genes from overlapping. RSCU values for the N. hainanensis mitochondrial genome indicate preferential utilization of codons ending in A/U (NNA/NNU), consistent with the elevated A + T content observed at third codon positions in its PCGs. The Ka/Ks values of all 13 PCGs are less than 1, indicating purifying selection, and meaning that genes are eliminated as disadvantageous when non-synonymous mutations occur during the process of species evolution. In the mitochondrial genome, the Ka/Ks value of cox1 is the lowest, indicating that it is the gene with the highest conservation, while atp8 is a gene with a relatively fast evolutionary rate.

In the mitochondrial genome of N. hainanensis, 22 tRNA genes, except for trnS1, which cannot form the typical cloverleaf structure due to the absence of the DHU arm, are capable of folding into the typical cloverleaf secondary structure. The absence of the DHU arm in trnS1 is similarly documented in other Metazoa. Compared to other species within Mezirinae, N. hainanensis exhibits conserved features in tRNA gene length, quantity, anticodon composition, and genomic arrangement. In N. hainanensis, certain tRNAs contain G-U and A-A mismatches, which are tolerated during tRNA folding. These mismatches are frequently observed in insect mitochondrial genomes and can be resolved through self-editing mechanisms without impairing transcriptional functionality.

The phylogenetic tree indicates that Neuroctenus and Mezira share a close phylogenetic relationship, consistent with previous research findings. Additionally, the phylogenetic trees consistently place Aradacanthia at the base of Aradidae, indicating that species of this genus represent an early-diverging lineage. The inferred phylogenetic relationships within Pentatomomorpha are as follows: (Aradoidea + (Pentatomoidea + (Lygaeoidea + (Coreoidea + Pyrrhocoroidea)))). The phylogenetic analyses strongly support Aradoidea as a monophyletic group at the base of Pentatomomorpha, congruent with prior studies. For instance, Li proposed a similar Pentatomomorpha topology of (Aradoidea + (Pentatomoidea + (Pyrrhocoroidea + Coreoidea + Lygaeoidea))), while supporting the monophyly of both Aradoidea and Pentatomoidea. Morphologically, Aradoidea differs from other Pentatomomorpha species by the absence of abdominal trichobothria. However, its classification within Pentatomomorpha is justified by shared derived features with Trichophora, including pulvilli, tubular salivary glands, egg structures, and seminal receptacles. Consequently, Aradoidea is recognized as the sister group to all other Pentatomomorpha species, representing a specialized basal clade within this suborder. These morphological conclusions align with the phylogenetic results of this study. Both morphological and molecular phylogenetic evidence collectively affirm the monophyly of Aradoidea.

The study strongly supports the monophyly of Pentatomomorpha, consistent with both morphological trait analyses and molecular data. Regarding phylogenetic relationships among Pentatomomorpha superfamilies, the topology (Aradoidea + (Pentatomoidea + remaining Trichophora)) is widely accepted. However, relationships within Trichophora:specifically among Pyrrhocoroidea, Coreoidea, and Lygaeoidea:remain highly contentious, with conflicting hypotheses proposed across studies. For example, Xu et al. suggested a topology of (Coreoidea + (Pyrrhocoroidea + Lygaeoidea)), but the sister-group relationship between Pyrrhocoroidea and Lygaeoidea did not receive high support. Hua et al. proposed a hypothesis of (Pyrrhocoroidea + (Lygaeoidea + Coreoidea)), which is inconsistent with the results of this study. Henry, based on morphological characteristics, concluded that the relationships among the three superfamilies were ((Coreoidea + Pyrrhocoroidea) + Lygaeoidea),), a view shared by Tian et al. Yuan et al., through phylogenetic analysis based on mitochondrial genome data, supported the relationship (Lygaeoidea + (Pyrrhocoroidea + Coreoidea)), which is essentially consistent with the results of this study.

Although this study drew a series of conclusions based on current molecular phylogenetic analysis methods, it is important to note that these conclusions should be approached with caution. This is because most existing phylogenetic analysis methods are largely based on the neutral theory and the molecular clock hypothesis, both of which have been increasingly questioned in recent years. Therefore, the conclusions of this study should remain open-ended, and future research should incorporate additional molecular data and new theoretical frameworks to further validate and expand upon the current findings.
Conclusion

This study obtained the mitochondrial genome sequence of N. hainanensis and conducted a preliminary analysis of its mitochondrial genomic composition and structural characteristics, and analyzed the phylogenetic position of Aradoidea within Pentatomomorpha. The results effectively supplement the molecular data of Aradidae, and are of significant importance for the molecular identification of N. hainanensis, the study of population genetics, and the in-depth exploration of the phylogenetic relationships within Aradidae. However, due to the limitations of current methodologies and technical means, these findings still need to be further verified through additional research.
Methods
Insect sources and DNA extraction

Adult samples of N. hainanensis were collected from Wuzhishan, Hainan Province, China (18.9136 N, 109.6881 E), immersed in anhydrous ethanol, and stored at - 20  C. Samples were deposited in the Insect Collection of Inner Mongolia Normal University. Genomic DNA was extracted from thoracic tissue using the Universal Genomic DNA Kit (CWBIO, Beijing, China) following the instructions.
Mitochondrial genome sequencing, assembly and annotation

Qualified samples were sequenced by Berry Genomics Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China) using the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform for paired-end (PE) sequencing (150 bp read length). Raw data were quality-controlled with fastp software to trim adapters, remove primer sequences, filter low-quality reads, and exclude reads with more than 5% N-content, generating 6 Gb of clean data. Clean data were assembled with SPAdes v3.14.1 (http://bioinf.spbau.ru/spades).

The mitochondrial genome was initially annotated using MITOS(http://mitos2.bioinf.uni-leipzig.de/index.py) with the following parameters: genetic code = 05-invertebrate, reference = RefSeq 89 Metazoa, and remaining parameters were retained as default. Annotations were imported into Geneious Prime v11 for comparative analysis with the published Aradidae mitochondrial genome (Neuroctenus parus NC_012459), enabling manual adjustment of gene boundaries.
Bioinformatic analysis

MITOS was utilized to predict protein-coding, tRNA, and rRNA genes and to perform de-redundancy processing on its initial predictions. tRNAscan-SE (http://www.http://lowelab.ucsc.edu/tRNAscan-SE/) was used for tRNA localization, and Adobe Illustrator 2024 was employed to illustrate tRNA structures. The online server CGView Server (https://cgview.ca/) was used to visualize the mitochondrial map. The frequency of each codon in protein-coding genes was compared to the total number of codons to calculate relative synonymous codon usage (RSCU), where an RSCU value > 1 indicated codon preference, with higher values reflected stronger bias. MEGA and PhyloSuite were utilized to analyze RSCU, base composition, codon preference, and gene spacing/gene overlap regions. AT-skew and GC-skew were calculated as: AT-skew = (A - T)/(A + T) and GC-skew = (G - C)/(G + C). Nonsynonymous-to-synonymous substitution rate ratios (Ka/Ks) of PCGs in Aradidae were analyzed using DnaSP v5.10.01. AliGROOVE v1.08 was used to assess the heterogeneity of each dataset (https://github.com/PatrickKueck/AliGROOVE).
Phylogenetic analysis

The mitochondrial genome sequence of N. hainanensis obtained from sequencing was combined with 51 species from 5 superfamilies in Pentatomomorpha as the ingroup. Two species from Cimicomorpha were used as the outgroup (Supplementary file 7). Phylosuite v1.2.3 was used to extract PCGs (protein-coding genes) and AA (amino acids). Multiple sequence alignments for PCGs and AA were performed using MAFFT 7.402. Aligned PCGs were refined with MACSE. Subsequently, the Gbloks was employed to trim, remove, and align ambiguous fragments from both the optimized PCGs and AA sequences. These sequences were then imported into FASconCAT-G v1.04 software for gene concatenation. Three phylogenetic datasets were generated: (1) a nucleotide dataset incorporating all three codon positions of the 13 protein-coding genes (PCG123); (2) a nucleotide dataset excluding third codon positions (PCG12); and (3) an amino acid sequence dataset (AA).

Partitioning of concatenated datasets was performed using ModelFinder, followed by model selection to identify the best-fit evolutionary model (Supplementary file 8-13). The BI tree was constructed with Exabayes v1.5.1 under the selected model, using MCMC runs of 10,000,000 generations, a sampling frequency of 1000, and discarding 25% of the burn-in samples. Convergence was confirmed when the average standard deviation of split frequencies (ASDSF) reached <= 0.01. The ML tree was constructed using IQ-TREE v2, with "Number of Bootstrap" set to 100,000, a sampling frequency of 1000, and "Bootstrap" set to Ultrafast. Final tree visualization was refined using TVBOT (https://www.chiplot.online/tvbot.html).

passages.text: When should the nephrologist think about genetics in patients with glomerular diseases?
ABSTRACT

This review discusses the significance of genetics in diagnosing glomerular diseases. Advances in genetic testing, particularly next-generation sequencing, have improved the accessibility and accuracy of diagnosing monogenic diseases, allowing for targeted gene panels and whole-exome/genome sequencing to identify genetic variants associated with glomerular diseases. Key indicators for considering a genetic cause include the age of onset, extrarenal features, family history, and inconclusive kidney biopsy results. Early-onset diseases, for instance, have a higher likelihood of being genetically caused, while extrarenal manifestations can also suggest an underlying genetic condition. A thorough family history can reveal patterns of inheritance that point to monogenic causes, although complexities like incomplete penetrance, skewed X inactivation and mosaicism can complicate the assessment. Also, autosomal recessive conditions imply asymptomatic parents, making genetic suspicion less likely, while de novo mutations can occur without any family history, further obscuring genetic assessment. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is characterized by podocyte injury and depletion, presenting in various forms, including primary, genetic, and secondary FSGS. Accurate classification of FSGS patients based on clinical and histological features is essential for guiding treatment decisions, optimizing therapeutic plans, avoiding unnecessary immunosuppression, and predicting relapse risk after kidney transplantation. Overall, a clinicopathological approach, enriched by genetic testing, offers a precise framework for diagnosis and management in glomerular diseases. Future directions for research and clinical practice include potential advancements in genetic testing and personalized medicine, which could further improve diagnostic precision and individualized treatment strategies.
INTRODUCTION

Kidney disease represents a major global health challenge, with its prevalence on a steady rise, now ranking as the seventh leading cause of mortality worldwide. Approximately 700 million individuals globally are affected by chronic kidney disease (CKD). A recent analysis from the European Renal Association registry revealed that in 2019, among prevalent patients receiving kidney replacement therapy (KRT), inherited kidney diseases (IKDs) and congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUTs) accounted for 18.5% of cases, while glomerulonephritis was responsible for 18.7%. Notably, IKD-CAKUT emerged as the leading cause of kidney failure in women (21.6%). However, these figures are likely underestimated, as they reflect 2019 data and a pan-European perspective. Genetic testing availability varied across Europe at that time (and still does) and has since improved, suggesting that a portion of patients diagnosed with 'glomerulonephritis' or 'other diseases' may, in fact, have underlying genetic conditions. This would position IKD-CAKUT as the most prevalent cause of KRT.

annotations.text: congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract

passages.text: A key reason for the higher prevalence of IKD-CAKUT is that these patients often present with fewer severe comorbidities, tend to be younger, and have longer survival rates compared with others on KRT. Beyond demographic considerations, the advent of next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies has made genetic testing more accessible and affordable, providing an invaluable tool for diagnosing glomerular diseases.

Today, genetic testing options range from targeted gene panels, which focus on specific exonic regions linked to glomerular diseases, to more comprehensive approaches like exome sequencing, which examines all protein-coding regions, and whole-genome sequencing (WGS), which covers the entire genome. Recent technological advancements, particularly the development of long-read sequencing, have enhanced diagnostic precision. Short-read sequencing, while highly accurate and cost-effective for identifying small variants such as single-nucleotide variants and small indels, struggles with detecting large structural variants or long repetitive sequences. However, it is worth noting that short-read WGS shows a higher sensitivity for detecting structural variants than whole-exome sequencing (WES) or other targeted approaches, as it can detect the intergenic breakpoints of balanced structural variants, such as inversions. In contrast, long-read sequencing overcomes these limitations by reading longer DNA fragments, which also enables the detection of complex genomic rearrangements, although it remains costlier at present. These innovations are pushing genetic testing toward more comprehensive, precise, and personalized diagnostics.

In this review we will explore the key indicators (Fig. 1) that suggest an inherited glomerulopathy, address the challenges associated with genetic testing, and highlight the benefits of achieving a precise diagnosis.
Key features to elicit a request for a genetic test for glomerular disease.
FEATURES SUGGESTING A GLOMERULAR DISEASE OF GENETIC ORIGIN
Age of onset

Early onset of glomerular disease should prompt suspicion of a genetic origin, although considerable variability exists, reflecting the broad phenotypic spectrum observed across different conditions. Recognizing this variability is essential for guiding clinical decisions regarding the need and timing of genetic testing.

In recent years, the number of genes implicated in genetic steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) has expanded significantly. Multiple guidelines for genetic screening have been proposed, particularly for congenital and infantile cases, where the likelihood of identifying a monogenic cause is higher. The prevalence of pathogenic variants has been shown to inversely correlate with the age of onset. For example, a 100% detection rate was reported for congenital nephrotic syndrome (with most pathogenic variants found in the NPHS1 gene), 57% in infantile onset, and 24%-36% in childhood and adolescent onset (mainly NPHS2) in a cohort of 125 patients. Although the diagnostic yield has traditionally been lower for adult-onset cases, disease-causing pathogenic variants have also been detected, with an estimated 8%-14% of adult-onset SRNS/FSGS, including both familial and sporadic cases.

Pathogenic variants in non-collagen genes tend to be found in patients with proteinuria onset before the age of 30, while heterozygous pathogenic variants in collagen genes may manifest even beyond the fifth decade of life. FSGS is a well-known pathological finding in Alport syndrome, which is marked by a wide phenotypic spectrum and variable age of onset depending on the mode of inheritance. Variants in collagen genes (COL4A3, COL4A4, COL4A5) are among the most common disease-causing variants identified in adult patients with sporadic SRNS/FSGS, accounting for 44%-56% of cases.

The advent of high-throughput sequencing technologies in adult CKD cohorts has reinforced the importance of achieving an accurate diagnosis, even in adulthood. A study of 1623 CKD patients, categorized into specific clinical disease groups with a median age of 55 years, found a diagnostic yield of 16.9% among those with proteinuric diseases suggestive of primary glomerulopathy. Variants in COL4A3/COL4A4/COL4A5 were responsible for 31.8% of positive cases, while high-risk APOL1 genotypes were identified in 45.5% of cases. In a recent Spanish cohort of 818 adult patients under 45 years with CKD stage 4-5 of unknown origin, the two leading diagnosed conditions were Alport syndrome spectrum (35%) and genetic podocytopathies (19%).

Previous research from our group demonstrated that seven genes accounted for 66% of positive genetic tests among individuals with CKD onset before 30 years of age. Interestingly, five of these genes (COL4A3/COL4A4/COL4A5, PKD1, and PKD2) were also among the six most frequently detected in an adult cohort studied by Groopman et al., with PKHD1 and HNF1B more common in the younger cohort, while UMOD was more prevalent in older individuals.

IKD and CAKUT are the leading causes of kidney failure in patients younger than 20 years (41% of cases), but their incidence peaks in patients over 45, mainly due to autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD).

Understanding that genetic kidney diseases can present at any age emphasizes the need for greater awareness and the importance of genetic testing across all age groups. However, given that the prevalence of genetic kidney diseases is higher among younger patients, it is particularly important to consider genetic causes in children and young adults with CKD as well as in patients with CKD of unknown etiology, especially those wait-listed for kidney transplantation for whom a living-related donor is being considered.
Extrarenal features

Glomerular diseases of genetic origin frequently involve multiple systems and are not confined to the kidneys. Notably, monogenic disorders with recessive inheritance patterns often result in rare syndromes that strongly suggest an underlying genetic condition. Table 1 offers a detailed overview of the extrarenal manifestations commonly associated with genetically driven glomerular diseases (complementopathies beyond atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) are not included due to its complex inheritance). Some key examples are discussed below.

Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the GLA gene, leading to the accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb-3) throughout the body. Ophthalmologically, this results in cornea verticillata (subepithelial spiral opacities that do not impair vision), posterior cataracts, and tortuosity of the retinal vessels. In the integumentary system, Gb-3 deposits lead to angiokeratomas and hypohidrosis or anhidrosis, contributing to heat intolerance. The gastrointestinal system may be affected by recurrent abdominal pain, nausea, and diarrhea due to vascular and autonomic dysfunction. Additionally, patients often experience progressive sensorineural hearing loss, which is sometimes accompanied by tinnitus and vertigo. These features compound the primary organ involvement affecting the kidneys, heart, and brain.
Alport syndrome is often associated with high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, anterior lenticonus, anterior subcapsular cataracts, and punctate keratopathy.

Frasier syndrome results from pathogenic variants in the WT1 gene, which encodes a transcription factor involved in renal and gonadal development. Systemic manifestations include male pseudohermaphroditism, ambiguous genitalia, hypospadias, cryptorchidism, gonadoblastoma, and, in rare cases, nephroblastoma (Wilms' tumor).

Nail-patella syndrome, caused by pathogenic variants in the LMX1B gene and inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, presents with a range of extrarenal features such as hypoplastic or absent patellae, dystrophic nails, elbow dysplasia, iliac horn dysplasia, and open-angle glaucoma. Interestingly, some individuals with this condition may exhibit no renal symptoms at all.
The presence of such extrarenal manifestations should raise the suspicion of an underlying genetic condition and warrant the consideration of genetic testing.
Family history

When evaluating the potential for a monogenic cause of glomerular disease, a detailed family history is a critical tool. However, several genetic factors can complicate the family history, making the monogenic suspicion less apparent. Complex inheritance patterns, incomplete penetrance, and mechanisms such as X-inactivation can obscure how glomerular diseases manifest across different family members.

Monogenic glomerular diseases can follow various inheritance patterns. For instance, autosomal Alport syndrome is inherited in a semi-dominant manner, where individuals with biallelic pathogenic variants exhibit more severe disease than those with a single, monoallelic variant, who tend to experience milder symptoms. In the autosomal dominant form of the disease, where only one mutated allele is needed to cause illness, the condition can appear across multiple generations, with very variable severity. Additionally, incomplete penetrance can result in the presence of the mutated allele in asymptomatic family members, giving the impression that the disease skips a generation.

A more severe form of Alport syndrome is X-linked, where males typically present more severe symptoms, and females may display milder disease due to X-inactivation. X-inactivation occurs when one copy of the X chromosome is randomly inactivated in early female embryonic cells. However, skewed inactivation may favor either the wild-type or mutated allele, influencing disease expression. In such cases, females can exhibit varying severity depending on which X chromosome is inactivated in the majority of cells.

Alport syndrome presents yet another pattern of inheritance, as exemplified by autosomal recessive Alport syndrome. In autosomal recessive conditions, affected family members are typically siblings, while parents are asymptomatic carriers. As a result, a family history of kidney disease may be absent, making the suspicion of a genetic condition less likely. However, because autosomal recessive diseases are often severe, early presentation of the disease can raise suspicion of a genetic cause. In this case parents may not be asymptomatic and can be considered to have autosomal dominant Alport syndrome.

Another complicating factor are de novo pathogenic variants, which arise spontaneously either in a parental germ cell or during embryonic development. De novo variants can obscure genetic suspicion, as they occur without any prior family history, making it challenging to identify a genetic basis for the disease. Additionally, de novo cases may exhibit mild clinical features due to mosaicism, where the disease-causing variant is present in only a proportion of cells. Mosaicism must be considered during reproductive genetic counseling for the healthy parents of a child with a de novo variant in a gene associated with an autosomal dominant glomerular disease. While parents may be reassured that the de novo variant poses no risk of recurrence in future children, there is still a possibility of having another affected child due to germinal restricted mosaicism, which may not be detectable by conventional blood-targeted genetic testing.

Given these complexities, nephrologists must take a thorough, multi-generational family history:spanning at least three generations:inquiring not only about known kidney diseases but also potential extrarenal features.
Kidney biopsy

Kidney biopsy (KB) is a cornerstone diagnostic tool in nephrology, with an estimated diagnostic accuracy of 80%. Recent studies indicate that incorporating genetic testing for patients with inconclusive KB results can significantly enhance etiological diagnosis. A single-center study examining the use of exome sequencing in routine clinical practice found that it enabled diagnosis in 40% of patients with previously inconclusive KB, with Alport spectrum-related nephropathy being the most frequently identified genetic disorder. Importantly, the diagnostic yield increased to 70% among patients with a family history of kidney disease. The study cohort, composed predominantly of younger patients, limits the generalizability of these findings to older populations. Nonetheless, the higher prevalence of familial kidney disease observed in the genetically solved group compared with the genetically unresolved group reinforces that a positive family history remains a critical factor in diagnosing genetic kidney disease. Moreover, the predominant lesions observed in KB aligned with the genetic diagnoses of glomerular and tubulointerstitial diseases. Typical histological findings for glomerular genetic conditions are presented in Table 1; however, for several conditions the histological findings are non-specific.

It is important to note that a recent report estimated that up to 1 in 106 individuals in the general population carry heterozygous pathogenic variants in the COL4A3 or COL4A4 gene. However, the pathogenicity assessment of these variants was conducted using Varsome, a semi-automated online prediction tool, which at that time overestimated pathogenicity. This overestimation arose from the inclusion of criteria such as PP2 and PP5, which ClinGen recommended removing from the original ACMG/AMP guidelines due to concerns about double counting and the potential for errors in variant classification. Although a more precise assessment of the frequency of individuals with a pathogenic variant in COL4A3/COL4A4 is needed, these remain the most common pathogenic variants in genes associated with monogenic glomerular diseases. Furthermore, these genes exhibit incomplete penetrance. Taken together, these factors have implications for the rare cases in which genetic testing is performed prior to KB; finding a heterozygous pathogenic variant in COL4A3 or COL4A4 alone may not be diagnostic, as the patient might harbor a variant in these genes alongside an undiagnosed glomerulopathy.
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis

FSGS is a histological pattern of kidney injury that can arise from a variety of underlying causes and mechanisms, all of which share a common event: podocyte injury and depletion. Accurate identification of the etiological process leading to FSGS is crucial for effective treatment. Consequently, a clinicopathological approach has been recommended, classifying FSGS into primary, genetic, secondary, and FSGS of undetermined cause.

Primary FSGS is an immunologically driven disease that typically presents with full-blown nephrotic syndrome of sudden onset. Under electron microscopy, diffuse podocyte foot process effacement affecting >80% of the glomerular capillary surface is observed. These cases exhibit a high recurrence rate after kidney transplantation, which differentiates them from other FSGS types. Recently, anti-nephrin antibodies were identified in a subset of patients with minimal change disease and recurrent FSGS post-transplant. Furthermore, anti-nephrin and anti-slit diaphragm antibodies were observed in kidney biopsies from adult patients with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome and FSGS lesions under high-resolution microscopy. These findings support an autoimmune etiology, suggesting susceptibility to immunosuppressive therapy and opening avenues for precision therapies in the future.

Secondary FSGS arises from a variety of etiologies, including conditions that impose excessive stress on the glomerular filtration barrier (maladaptive forms) or directly injure podocytes (due to drugs, infections, etc.). Patients with secondary FSGS may exhibit varying levels of proteinuria but, unlike primary FSGS, typically maintain normal serum albumin levels and do not develop full nephrotic syndrome. Electron microscopy in secondary FSGS shows segmental foot process effacement, usually affecting less than 40% of the glomerular capillary surface. Maladaptive forms often occur in conditions with reduced nephron mass (e.g. low birth weight, renal dysplasia, reflux nephropathy) or increased glomerular filtration rate exceeding glomerular capacity (e.g. obesity, uncontrolled hypertension, sleep apnea, high protein intake). Other causes of secondary FSGS include virus-associated FSGS (e.g. due to HIV, CMV, or parvovirus B19) and drug-induced FSGS (e.g. caused by TOR inhibitors, lithium, pamidronate, anti-VEGF agents), which generally improve with infection resolution or cessation of the causative drug.

Genetic FSGS results from pathogenic variants in genes that encode proteins crucial to podocyte structure or function, or the glomerular basement membrane (GBM). Clinical presentation varies, with some cases resembling primary FSGS with full nephrotic syndrome, while others present with proteinuria and normal serum albumin, similar to secondary FSGS. Although genetic forms of FSGS often have childhood onset, the wide phenotypic spectrum means that adult-onset genetic FSGS cannot be ruled out solely based on age.

FSGS of undetermined cause refers to cases without a clear genetic or secondary origin, in the absence of nephrotic syndrome or diffuse foot process effacement on electron microscopy. These cases are thought to result from genetic or secondary causes yet to be identified.

Accurate classification of FSGS patients based on clinical and histological features is essential for guiding treatment decisions, optimizing therapeutic plans, avoiding unnecessary immunosuppression, and predicting relapse risk after kidney transplantation.

The role of genetic testing in adult FSGS cases remains uncertain. The 2021 KDIGO guidelines recommend case-by-case consideration for genetic testing (Table 2). A positive family history or syndromic features also increase the likelihood of a genetic diagnosis. Genetic testing is also advised for patients with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, as nearly 42% of these cases have an underlying genetic cause, and a prompt diagnosis could enable the discontinuation of immunosuppressive therapy. In patients of African ancestry, APOL1 genetic risk variants are associated with a significantly increased risk of developing FSGS, and kidneys from APOL1 high-risk donors have reduced graft survival compared with non-risk donors. Thus, genetic testing in donors of African ancestry is essential to inform both the donor's risk of chronic kidney disease and the recipient's allograft survival.

Recurrence in kidney transplantation

Unlike glomerular diseases of non-genetic origin, genetic glomerular diseases typically do not recur in the transplant graft, as the new organ does not carry the mutations present in the original damaged kidney. However, there are some exceptions.

Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome is a condition marked by thrombotic microangiopathy, which leads to hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. The recurrence rate in kidney transplants is notably high, ranging from 50% to 80%, due to genetic defects in the complement system, involving genes like CFH, CFI, CD46, CFB, and C3. If a family member is considering becoming a kidney donor, it is crucial to exclude the presence of the pathogenic variant in the donor, given the significant risk of recurrence. Prophylactic treatment with eculizumab (a complement inhibitor) may reduce the risk of recurrence.

In some genetic diseases, an 'immune' recurrence may occur after transplantation. Rare examples include X-linked Alport syndrome in males, recessive Alport syndrome, and the nephrotic syndrome of Finnish type. In these rare cases, the recipient's immune system fails to recognize antigens in the graft and produces antibodies against key parts of the nephron, leading to severe kidney damage.
POSSIBLE RESULTS OF GENETIC TESTING

Genetic testing in glomerular diseases can yield a range of results, each with specific implications for diagnosis and management. A positive result indicates the presence of a pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in a gene associated with either monoallelic or biallelic disease. This finding suggests a clear monogenic cause for the glomerular disease, especially if supported by strong evidence of gene-disease association, such as that provided by ClinGen, a National Institutes of Health (NIH)-funded resource that defines the clinical validity of gene-disease relationships for precision medicine.

Establishing the disease mechanism is also crucial, since some diseases are caused by loss-of-function variants whereas others are caused by gain-of-function variants. Moreover, variants in some genes may be only pathogenic if they impact specific protein domains. For example, the INF2 gene encodes a formin family protein involved in actin cytoskeleton remodeling, mitochondrial dynamics, and microtubule stabilization. Monoallelic gain-of-function variants in INF2 affecting the diaphanous inhibitory domain (DID) encoded by exons 2-4 are associated with autosomal dominant FSGS. However, loss-of-function variants or missense variants outside this domain are not disease-causing.

When a genetic test identifies a variant of uncertain significance (VUS), it should be regarded as a non-diagnostic result, since the clinical significance of the variant remains unclear. This uncertainty arises from several factors, including the high prevalence of rare variants across the genome and the incomplete understanding of the functional impact of many variants. Importantly, acting on a VUS can lead to significant hazards, such as misdiagnosis or inappropriate treatment decisions. For instance, a misdiagnosis based on a VUS could lead to unwarranted interventions, such as immunosuppressive therapy or predictive testing in asymptomatic family members, potentially causing harm. These considerations emphasize the importance of treating a VUS as a hypothesis rather than a definitive result until sufficient evidence is available to reclassify it as either likely benign or likely pathogenic. Regular monitoring for updates on the variant's classification is crucial, as evidence from co-segregation studies in multi-generational families, reports of the same variant in well-characterized cases, or functional studies can aid in its reclassification. Clinicians can also collaborate with genetic experts through platforms like GeneMatcher to re-evaluate variant classifications over time as new evidence emerges.

Another complex scenario arises when genetic findings indicate susceptibility to disease rather than causation of a Mendelian disorder. As previously mentioned, APOL1 risk variants, G1 and G2, are strongly associated with increased risk of FSGS and other kidney diseases, particularly in individuals of African ancestry. However, the presence of these APOL1 risk variants does not invariably lead to disease, as environmental and other genetic factors modulate risk and many healthy individuals are homozygous or compound heterozygous for APOL1 risk variants. Being G1/G1, G2/G2 or G1/G2 carries implications for affected individuals and their family members, as these findings can inform personalized monitoring strategies but should not be equated with a definitive genetic diagnosis. It is crucial to clearly communicate the distinction between genetic susceptibility and Mendelian inheritance to patients and their families to prevent undue anxiety or unnecessary medical interventions.

A negative result does not exclude the possibility of a monogenic cause for glomerular disease. Technical limitations, such as difficulties in detecting structural variants or variants in non-coding regions, may contribute to negative results. In cases with a strong clinical suspicion of a genetic cause, further testing methods, such as whole-genome sequencing or long-read sequencing, should be considered. Additionally, periodic reanalysis of genomic data is beneficial as advancements in variant-calling algorithms or new gene discoveries may later identify previously undetectable variants. Other inheritance models, such as mitochondrial or polygenic inheritance, or even non-genetic causes, should also be explored to fully understand the patient's condition.
Benefits of genetic testing

Accurate diagnosis is critical for all conditions, but it holds particular importance in glomerular diseases. In the absence of a genetic or precise histological diagnosis, patients with proteinuria are likely to receive corticosteroids and immunosuppressive drugs, which carry significant side effects. A positive genetic test can prevent unnecessary treatment, allowing management with antiproteinuric agents alone.

Genetic testing is increasingly recognized as a critical tool in kidney transplantation, with growing implications for the evaluation and management of both transplant recipients and living donors. It offers several benefits as it identifies patients needing heightened surveillance or targeted interventions for extrarenal manifestations and reassures when recurrence risk is low. For living donors, it is pivotal in evaluating related donors, informing eligibility decisions, and safeguarding their long-term health by detecting predisposition to kidney dysfunction. For most genetic glomerular diseases, disease recurrence is uncommon; however, rare immune responses may occur. For instance, anti-nephrin antibodies have been reported in Finnish-type nephrotic syndrome, and anti-GBM antibodies have been observed in rare cases of Alport syndrome. These responses represent immune reactions to unfamiliar proteins rather than true disease relapses.

CONCLUSION

In summary, integrating genetic testing into the diagnostic process for glomerular diseases enhances diagnostic accuracy, especially in cases with inconclusive kidney biopsy results. While kidney biopsy remains essential, genetic testing can clarify the etiology of conditions like FSGS, helping tailor treatment by identifying when immunosuppressive therapies may be unnecessary. Genetic results require careful interpretation, as positive findings may pinpoint a monogenic cause, while variants of uncertain significance need ongoing evaluation. Negative results do not rule out genetic causes, suggesting further testing may be necessary. Overall, a clinicopathological approach, enriched by genetic testing, offers a precise framework for diagnosis and management in glomerular diseases. Future directions for research and clinical practice include potential advancements in genetic testing and personalized medicine, which could further improve diagnostic precision and individualized treatment strategies.

passages.text: Optimization ultrasonic-assisted aqueous two-phase extraction of glabridin from licorice root and its activity against the foodborne pathogen MRSA

This study aimed to extract glabridin (GLA) from licorice using an environmentally sustainable ultrasonic-assisted aqueous two-phase extraction method and to evaluate its efficacy. The extraction parameters were optimized through single-factor experiments and response surface methodology, resulting in a GLA content of 2049.51 mug/g under the conditions of 51 min ultrasonic time, 76  C ultrasonic temperature, and 640 W ultrasonic power. In vitro analyses demonstrated that licorice extract (1.6 mg/mL) and GLA (8 mug/g) exhibited rapid bactericidal activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Furthermore, both licorice extract and GLA showed significant disinfection activity against MRSA in models of pork spoilage and cooking utensils. Mechanistic studies revealed that GLA targets phospholipids, thereby disrupting the integrity and normal function of bacterial cell membranes. In conclusion, this study introduces an environmentally sustainable and effective method for obtaining a GLA-rich extract from licorice, which has potential applications in the food industry for addressing MRSA contamination.
Highlights
UA-ATPE was optimized by RSM in term with the extraction yields of GLA.
The antibacterial and disinfection activity of obtained extract and GLA was demonstrated in vitro.
The targeting of GLA to phospholipids against MRSA was clarified by MD simulation and ITC assay.
GLA disrupts cell membrane function anti MRSA mechanisms were elucidated.
Licorice extract and GLA may serve as safe additives to control bacterial contamination of foods.
Introduction

Foodborne diseases (FBD) are prevalent globally, with microbial contamination of food serving as a significant contributor to FBD incidence. Staphylococcus aureus, a well-known FBD pathogen, is commonly found in meats such as pork, chicken, and beef, and can even be detected on the surfaces of cutlery. This pathogen is responsible for a range of clinical symptoms, including vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. To mitigate the risk of FBD, chemical preservatives are typically employed to inhibit or control the proliferation of pathogenic microorganisms in food products. Nonetheless, there is increasing concern regarding the potential health risks associated with the use of these chemical preservatives (F.). Consequently, it is imperative to investigate safe and natural antibacterial agents as alternatives to conventional chemical preservatives in order to enhance food quality.

In recent years, natural preservatives derived from plants have garnered significant attention due to their antimicrobial and antioxidant properties, ease of degradation, and high safety profile. For instance, Dang et al. demonstrated that the incorporation of 6 % flavonoid-rich herbal extracts into fermented-bag sausages enhanced both their quality and safety. Similarly, Bajpai et al. isolated amentoflavone from Nandina domestica, which markedly reduced the cell counts of S. aureus and Escherichia coli in minced chicken meat and apple juice. These findings indicate that flavonoid-rich plant extracts hold potential as natural preservatives for improving food freshness and extending shelf life. Licorice (Glycyrrhiza uralensis Fisch), recognized as a plant with medicinal and nutritional properties, is frequently incorporated into traditional Chinese medicine formulations for the treatment of infections, including respiratory and dental diseases caused by viral or bacterial agents. This distinctive therapeutic application is primarily attributed to its bioactive constituents, particularly flavonoids. Among these, glabridin (GLA) is a significant flavonoid compound exhibiting notable antibacterial, antiviral, and anti-inflammatory properties. Previous studies have confirmed the antibacterial and antifungal efficacy of GLA against pathogens such as S. aureus, Bacillus subtilis, Escherichia coli, and Candida albicans, with minimum inhibitory concentrations (MIC) ranging from 8 to 250 mug/mL. Moreover, GLA has demonstrated a favorable safety profile; oral administration of 300 mg/day over a 12-week period in individuals with type 2 diabetes showed no adverse effects and significantly improved vascular function in healthy subjects. Consequently, licorice extract and GLA present as promising and safe additives for mitigating bacterial contamination in the food industry.

Currently, traditional solvent extraction still plays an important role in efficient extraction of flavonoid compounds from natural plants. However, the use of organic solvents in these conventional extraction methods frequently results in substantial environmental pollution and poses risks to human health. Recently, there has been a growing interest in aqueous two-phase extraction (ATPE) due to its cost-effectiveness, high efficiency, and environmentally sustainable characteristics. Furthermore, the presence of two immiscible solvents in aqueous two-phase system (ATPS) aids in streamlining the purification process, thereby minimizing the loss of desired constituents during impurity removal. As a result, ATPE has become widely utilized for the extraction and isolation of flavonoids, alkaloids, and polysaccharides.

Ultrasound-assisted extraction (UAE) is increasingly recognized as a significant emerging technology for the efficient extraction of natural active ingredients. UAE operates by transmitting pressure waves of varying frequencies (20-100 kHz) through different media, enhancing extraction efficiency by disrupting plant cell walls and altering temperature. Notably, Zhu et al. employed ultrasound-assisted aqueous two-phase extraction (UA-ATPE) to successfully extract significant quantities of flavonoids, including rutin, quercetin 3-beta-d-glucoside, and kaempferol 3-rutinoside, from jujube peels. Similarly, Zhou et al. demonstrated that UA-ATPE was more effective in extracting flavonoids from Lysionotus pauciflorus than traditional solvents such as water, ethanol, and 60 % ethanol, as well as UAE. This suggests that the integration of high-energy ultrasonic waves with the ATPS demixing effect may enhance flavonoid extraction. While methods such as ethanol/water extraction, UAE, supercritical fluid extraction, and ultrasound-assisted deep eutectic solvent extraction have been documented for the extraction of GLA from licorice, the application of UA-ATPE for this purpose remains unexplored. Additionally, existing research predominantly focuses on evaluating the broad pharmacological activities of extracts derived from natural plants, with limited systematic investigation into their antibacterial efficacy against foodborne pathogens.

This study focused on optimizing the extraction process of GLA from licorice utilizing UA-ATPE. The optimization was achieved through a combination of single-factor experiments and the application of a Box-Behnken design (BBD) within the framework of response surface methodology (RSM). Furthermore, the antibacterial and disinfectant properties of the extract against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) were evaluated, accompanied by an in-depth analysis of the underlying antibacterial mechanisms. This research not only introduces an efficient and environmentally sustainable method for the large-scale extraction of GLA from licorice but also highlights the potential of licorice extract and GLA as alternatives to conventional food preservatives and additives.

Licorice was procured from the Chinese herbal market in Harbin, China. The dried licorice roots were ground into powder using a pulverizer and subsequently stored in a desiccator at ambient temperature. Table 1 details the bacterial strains utilized in this study. S. aureus exhibits rapid proliferation at 37  C in Trypticase Soy Broth (TSB, Qingdao Hope Bio-technology). The antibacterial assays employed Mueller Hinton Broth (MHB, Qingdao Hope Bio-technology) as the culture medium. (NH4)2SO4, K2CO3, Na2CO3, NaH2PO4, and anhydrous ethanol were purchased from Tianli Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. (Tianjin, China). BCECF-AM, DISC3(5), and Laurdan were obtained from Merck (Shanghai, China). Glabridin was acquired from Chengdu Herbpurify Co., Ltd. (Chengdu, China).
HPLC analysis

(A) HPLC chromatograms of different samples. (I) standard analytes of GLA, (II) UA-ATPS extracts. (B) The phase diagrams of ethanol/salt systems at room temperature. (C) Scanning electron micrographs of licorice powder after extraction by (I) before extraction, (II) ethanol/(NH4)2SO4, (III) ethanol/NaH2PO4, (IV) ethanol/Na2CO3, and (V) ethanol/K2CO3.
Fig. 1

The samples were diluted with methanol and filtered through a 0.22 mum membrane filter. The GLA content was quantified using a Waters 2695 High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) system. Chromatographic separation was performed on a DiKMA Extend-C18 column (250 x 4.6 mm, 5 mum) at 25  C. The mobile phase was composed of acetonitrile (A) and 0.1 % phosphoric acid (B). Gradient elution was performed as follows: 35 % A from 0 to 33 min, 35-25 % A from 3 to 20, 25 % A from 20 to 21 min, 25-35 % A from 21 to 23 min, and 35 % A from 23 to 25 min. The flow rate was maintained at 0.6 mL/min, the detection wavelength was set to 280 nm, and the injection volume was 10 muL. Each sample was analyzed in triplicate. The results indicated that the HPLC retention time for GLA was 7.7 min (Fig. 1A). The regression equation for GLA was: Y = 27,477 X -75,519 (R2 = 0.997, X: GLA concentration, Y: peak area).
Preparation of ATPS

ATPS was constructed using absolute ethanol, salt, and purified water. The preparation process for ATPS involved dissolving a specified amount of salt in a given volume of water, followed by the immediate addition of a predetermined volume of ethanol, with thorough mixing until two phases were formed. The time required for phase formation and the stability of each ATPS were observed and recorded.
Phase diagram of ATPS

The phase diagram was prepared using the turbidimetric titration method. Initially, 3.5 g of various salts were dissolved in 10 mL of distilled water, and ethanol was added dropwise until the solution became turbid. Subsequently, distilled water was incrementally added until the solution regained clarity. The volumes of ethanol and distilled water added were meticulously recorded. This procedure of incremental addition of ethanol and distilled water was repeated 50 times to acquire sufficient data for the construction of a phase diagram.
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM)

Following treatment with different ATPS, including ethanol/(NH4)2SO4, ethanol/K2CO3, ethanol/Na2CO3, and ethanol/NaH2PO4, the morphology of licorice powders was examined using SEM (Hitachi, SU8010, Japan). The powders were dried and analyzed at a magnification of 8000 x .
Extraction of GLA with UA-ATPE

The effectiveness of salts, such as (NH4)2SO4, K2CO3, Na2CO3, and NaH2PO4, on the extraction yield of GLA was investigated using UA-ATPE during the preliminary screening of ATPS components. Based on the phase diagram, ATPS with a total mass of 35 g and varying ethanol mass fractions (20 %, 30 %, and 40 %) were prepared. Briefly, the appropriate quantities of salt, water, and 1 g of licorice powder were combined. Subsequently, different volumes of ethanol were added immediately, resulting in biphasic separation. Analysis of the supernatant was conducted following sonication for 30 min at 35  C and 720 W, to determine the content of GLA. In addition, the recovery rate and distribution coefficient (K) of GLA were determined using the following equation to measure extraction capacity: Recovery (%) = CtVt/(CtVt + CbVb) x 100, K = Ct/Cb. Where Ct and Cb represent the GLA concentration of the top and bottom phases respectively, and Vt and Vb are the volumes of the top and bottom phases respectively.
Optimization of extraction process
Single-factor experiment

The UA-ATPE process was optimized through a single-factor experiment utilizing ethanol/(NH4)2SO4 as solvent. Seven independent variables were assessed to establish the preliminary range: ethanol mass fraction (20 %, 25 %, 30 %, 35 %, 40 %), (NH4)2SO4 mass fraction (9 %, 11 %, 13 %, 15 %, 17 %), ultrasonic time (5, 20, 35, 50, 65 min), ultrasonic temperature (35, 45, 55, 65, 75, 85  C), ultrasonic power (50 %, 60 %, 70 %, 80 %, 90 %, 100 % x 720 W), particle size (10, 24, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120 mesh), and solid-to-liquid (1/10, 1/20, 1/30, 1/40, 1/50, 1/60 g/mL).
RSM experiments

Based on the outcomes of the single-factor experiment, the Box-Behnken design (BBD) was implemented using Design-Expert Version 8.0 software (Stat-Ease Inc., Minneapolis, MN, USA) across 17 randomized trials to optimize the GLA content in the extract. The experimental variables included ultrasonic time (X1, 50 +- 15 min), ultrasonic temperature (X2, 75 +- 10  C), and ultrasonic power (X3, 648 +- 72 W).
UPLC-MS/MS analysis

The licorice extracts were analyzed utilizing an UPLC-ESI-MS/MS (UPLC, ExionLC  AD, https://sciex.com.cn/) system. The chromatographic analysis was conducted on an Agilent SB-C18 column (1.8 mum, 2.1 mm x 100 mm). The mobile phase comprised solvent A, which was water with 0.1 % formic acid, and solvent B, which was acetonitrile with 0.1 % formic acid. The sample analysis followed a gradient program starting with 95 % solvent A and 5 % solvent B. Over a period of 9 min, a linear gradient was applied to reach 5 % solvent A and 95 % solvent B, and this composition was maintained for an additional 1 min. Subsequently, the mixture was adjusted to 95 % A and 5 % B over 1.1 min and held for 2.9 min. The flow rate was set to 0.35 mL per minute, and the column oven temperature was maintained at 40  C. An injection volume of 2 muL was utilized. The effluent was then directed to an ESI-triple quadrupole-linear ion trap mass spectrometer (QTRAP-MS).
Antibacterial activity assay

Licorice extract and GLA MICs were determined by broth microdilution based on the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) standards. Briefly, the drugs were subjected to serial twofold dilutions in MHB medium within 96-well plates and were immediately combined with an equal volume of bacterial suspension at a concentration of 1 x 106 CFUs/mL. Following an 18 h incubation period at 37  C, the MIC was identified as the lowest drug concentration that inhibited bacterial growth. Based on the MIC results, the minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) for S. aureus USA300 was ascertained by performing colony counts on TSA plates, with the MBC defined as the lowest drug concentration resulting in fewer than five colonies after a 24 h incubation at 37  C. All experiments were independently repeated three times, with at least three biological replicates per experiment.
Resistance development studies

Subsequently, the log-phase S. aureus USA300 bacterial solution was treated with 0.5 x MIC of GLA, vancomycin (as a negative control), and oxacillin sodium (as a positive control). The cultures were incubated at 37  C with shaking at 180 rpm for 24 h Cultures exceeding the MIC levels were transferred to drug-free broth, and the MIC was determined using twofold serial dilutions in 96-well microtiter plates. This procedure was repeated daily for 30 days, and the MIC of GLA was ultimately calculated as a fold increase relative to the initial value.
Time-dependent killing curve

Overnight cultured S. aureus USA300 was diluted into MHB medium at a ratio of 1:1000 and cultured at 37  C with continuous shaking (180 rpm) for 1 h (logarithmic phase) and 4 h (stationary phase). Then, licorice extract, GLA, vancomycin and PBS were added separately, after continuing incubation for 0, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 24 h, bacterial numbers were calculated with TSA plate colony counting method.
Food spoilage model

The efficacy of licorice extract and GLA as food preservatives was assessed using a pork spoilage model contaminated with S. aureus USA300. In this study, pork was divided into three groups, each consisting of four portions weighing 2.0 g. The spoilage model was established by inoculating each portion with 50 muL of an S. aureus USA300 suspension at a concentration of 1 x 104 CFUs per portion. Subsequently, the contaminated pork was treated with 50 muL of either PBS, licorice extract (1.25 g/kg), or GLA (20 mg/kg). After 24 h of incubation at 37  C, the pork samples were homogenized in 2 mL of sterilized PBS and plated on chromogenic agar specific for S. aureus to determine the bacterial load.
Cooking utensils model

Stationary phase cultures of S. aureus USA300 were washed with PBS and adjusted to 5 x 106 CFUs for further use. Sterile lunch boxes (n = 3 per group) were contaminated with 150 muL of S. aureus USA300. Following a 30 min incubation period, each contaminated area was treated with 100 muL of licorice extract (1.6 mg/mL) and GLA (16 mug/mL) for 10 min. The bacteria were then collected and plated on TSA plates to quantify the bacterial colonies.
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM)

S. aureus USA300 with an OD600nm = 0.5 were washed three times with PBS and resuspended, and immediately treated with GLA for 30 mins. Post-treatment, the S. aureus USA300 cells were collected via centrifugation and fixed using 2.5 % glutaraldehyde and 1 % osmium acid, respectively. The samples were then sectioned and stained with lead citrate and uranyl acetate to facilitate the observation of cell membrane alterations via TEM.
Antibacterial activity of the mixtures of GLA and phospholipids

To evaluate the antibacterial efficacy of 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phospho-(1'-rac-glycerol) sodium salt (POPG, >= 98 %, Sigma-Aldrich) on GLA, POPG was dissolved in methanol to achieve a final concentration range of 2-256 mug/mL. This solution was mixed with GLA at a final concentration range of 16-256 mug/mL in a 1:1 ratio within a 96-well plate, followed by the addition of a diluted S. aureus USA300 bacterial suspension. The impact of POPG addition on the MIC was assessed after incubation at 37  C for 18 h.
Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) assays

To further elucidate the interaction between POPG and GLA at 25  C, POPG (2 mmol/L) was injected into calorimetric cells containing GLA (0.2 mmol/L), with injections repeated 19 times at 150 s intervals. Data was processed using the software package with the MicroCal PEAQ ITC to calculate entropy (DeltaS), enthalpy (DeltaH), stoichiometry (n) and changes of and equilibrium dissociation constant (KD).
All-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations

The previously described full atom MD simulation based on GROMACS software package was slightly modified to study the interaction between GLA molecules and simulated bacterial plasma membranes. All the simulated systems were assigned for CHARMM36m forcefield, and the ligand GLA was assigned for Charmm CGenFF force field. CHARMM-GUI was used to construct the 128 POPG lipid bilayers, coupled with TIP3P water molecules. The system was then neutralized by the addition of Na+ ions. The final systems contained 43,242 atoms with a volume of dimensions 6.28 nm x 6.28 nm x 10.68 nm. To visualize membrane attachment and penetration, phospholipids are represented as chains, and GLA molecules are depicted as large spheres. A steepest descent algorithm was used to minimize the energy of the systems using a 50,000-step energy minimization. In the NVT ensemble, the system balances 200 ps at 300 K. Then the NPT ensemble was equilibrated for 10 ns at 300 K and 1 atm. During equilibration, heavy atoms were constrained by harmonics with a force constant of 1000 kJ mol-1 nm-2. All the production runs were carried out under the NPT ensemble. The production of simulations lasted for 200 ns. The details of MD simulations can be found in our previous work.
DNA extravasation assay

The S. aureus USA300 was cultured to logarithmic phase OD600nm = 1.8, adjusted to an OD600nm = 0.5 after washing three times with PBS, added GLA and cultured at 37  C for 0, 0.5, 1, 2, and 4 h. The positive control group was suspended with 0.1 % Triton X-100. Centrifuged the bacterial solution to take the supernatant, DNA content was finally measured with the microspectrophotometer (IMPLEN, Nanophotometer-N60).
Fluorescence assay

In all fluorescence assays, bacterial pretreatment has been performed with a similar protocol, choosing S. aureus USA300 as the indicator strain. Briefly, the overnight culture of S. aureus USA300 was washed three times with HEPES (5 mmol/L) and resuspended to obtain an OD600nm = 0.5. After incubation at 37  C for 30 min with the addition of fluorescent dyes, the fluorescence values after GLA (0, 8, 16, 32 mug/mL) treatment were measured by microplate reader (Molecular Devices, SpectraMax iD3).
Membrane integrity assay

Propidium iodide (PI, 10 nmol/L) was used to assess the membrane integrity of S. aureus USA300. The fluorescence values of each treatment group were measured under the conditions of an excitation wavelength of 535 nm and an emission wavelength of 615 nm.
Membrane fluidity assays

S. aureus USA300 were stained with Laurdan (10 nmol/L) and treated with GLA or benzyl alcohol for 30 mins. Laurdan GP was calculated with excitation at 350 nm and emission at 460 nm and 500 nm (Laurdan GP = (I460-I500)/(I460 + I500)).
Proton motive force (PMF) assay

The PMF was determined by the pH sensitive fluorescence probe BCECF-AM (10 mumol/L). S. aureus USA300 after treatment with GLA, the excitation and emission wavelengths of the microplate reader were set to 488 nm and 535 nm, respectively, to determine the fluorescence values.
Membrane depolarization assay

Membrane depolarization (Deltapsi) was evaluated by the fluorescence probe DISC3(5) (10 mumol/L). The dissipation membrane potential of S. aureus USA300 was measured by an excitation wavelength of 622 nm and an emission wavelength of 670 nm in the presence of GLA.
Total ROS measurement

The DCFH-DA probe was added in S. aureus USA300 and the procedures followed the manufacturer's instructions (Beyotime, China). After incubating with GLA for 1 h, the fluorescence value was measured using microplate reader at an excitation wavelength of 488 nm and an emission wavelength of 525 nm.
ATP levels assay

S. aureus USA300 was adjusted to OD600nm = 0.5 and subjected to varying concentrations of GLA (0, 8, 16, 32 mug/mL). Intracellular ATP levels were quantified utilizing an ATP assay kit (Beyotime, China).
Statistical analysis

Figures for this study were drawn by Figdraw, GraphPad Prism 8 (GraphPad Software, Inc., San Diego, CA), or Biorender. Data were subjected to statistical analysis and the t-test and two-way ANOVA test were conducted by GraphPad Prism 8 software. The values were reported as means+-standard deviation (SD). Sample size (n) for each statistical analysis was 3. p < 0.05 was considered significant.
Results and discussion
Phase diagrams of the selected ATPSs

Currently, short-chain alcohol salt systems have emerged as a prevalent and cost-effective ATPS for the extraction of active plant ingredients, attributed to their superior phase separation capabilities, high selectivity, low cost, low viscosity, ease of recycling, and environmental sustainability. Typically, methanol does not readily form ATPSs with all salts, and its phase separation process is notably slow. In contrast, inorganic salts such as (NH4)2SO4, NaH2PO4, Na2CO3, and K2CO3 readily form ATPSs with ethanol. Consequently, this study investigates the phase diagrams of four ATPSs: ethanol/(NH4)2SO4, ethanol/NaH2PO4, ethanol/Na2CO3, and ethanol/K2CO3. As illustrated in Fig. 1B, two distinct regions delineated by curves are observed. The upper phase predominantly consists of an ethanol-rich aqueous solution, while the lower phase primarily comprises a salt-rich aqueous solution. When the mass fractions of salts are maintained at elevated levels, the extremum point of the ATPS curve is formed as the concentration of ethanol progressively increases. Correspondingly, high concentrations of ethanol also separate excess phase-forming salts. Importantly, when the mass fraction of ethanol is maintained in an appropriate range, the smaller the inorganic salt mass fraction, the easier the ATPS phase is formed. Therefore, the mass fractions of ethanol and phase-forming salts should first be selected from the region above the hyperbolic curve before the following experiments are performed. In the present study, (NH4)2SO4 exhibited good solubility and low cost, thus facilitating the potential applications of ATPS systems.

passages.text: The investigation of the impact of different types of salt on the extraction yield of GLA in licorice was extended based on the findings from phase diagrams (Fig. 1B). Among various ATPS, ethanol/(NH4)2SO4 demonstrated the highest extraction yield (Table 2). Specifically, when the proportions of ethanol and (NH4)2SO4 were increased to 48.64 % and 10.29 % respectively, the distribution coefficient is greater than 1 and the recovery rate was the highest (84.84 +- 0.33 %). It was shown that the ethanol/(NH4)2SO4 ATPS had the best GLA enrichment capacity for the ethanol phase. Moreover, Fig. 1C I shows that licorice powder surface was intact prior to ATPS treatment. Correspondingly, ethanol/(NH4)2SO4 caused the most severe damage to the plant surface compared with other ATPS (Fig. 1C II-V). This observation can be attributed to the role of (NH4)2SO4 in ATPS, which facilitates the disruption of cellular structures in the raw material, thereby enhancing the diffusion of intracellular chemicals into the surrounding solvent. Additionally, the salt ions in (NH4)2SO4 may form a weak complex with the plant's active ingredients, which prevents excessive binding and facilitates separation. Simultaneously, these salt ions can engage in moderate electrostatic interactions with target molecules, thereby enhancing the selectivity and efficiency of extraction. Consequently, ethanol/(NH4)2SO4 was identified as the optimal ATPS and selected for further investigation.

Effect of ATPS content on extraction efficiency

Effect of different (A) mass fractions of ethanol, (B) mass fractions of (NH4)2SO4, (C) extraction temperature, (D) extraction time, (E) extraction power, (F) particle size on extraction yields, and (G) solid-to-liquid ratio on extraction yields of GLA. Data are presented as the means +- SD. *** Most significant (p < 0.001). ** More significant (p < 0.01). * Significant (p < 0.05).
Fig. 2

The effect of anhydrous ethanol mass fraction on the extraction yield was explored using ethanol/(NH4)2SO4 as solvent. As the ethanol mass fraction increased from 31 % to 39 %, there was a gradual enhancement in the extraction yield of GLA, as depicted in Fig. 2A. However, a slight decline in the extraction yield was observed when the ethanol mass fraction exceeded this range. This phenomenon can be attributed to the reduction in the volume of the bottom phase as the ethanol volume increases. Consequently, an ethanol mass fraction of 35 % was deemed optimal. Salting-out effects play a pivotal role in the partitioning behavior within alcohol/salt systems. Therefore, the impact of varying concentrations of (NH4)2SO4 (9, 11, 13, 15 and 17 %) on the extraction yield was assessed at a constant ethanol concentration of 35 %. the extraction yield of GLA progressively increased with the (NH4)2SO4 mass fraction rising from 9 % to 13 %. Nevertheless, further addition of (NH4)2SO4, resulted in negligible improvement in the extraction yield, as the system reached saturation and excess (NH4)2SO4 led to salt precipitation. Consequently, the ATPS composed of 35 % ethanol (w/w) and 13 % (NH4)2SO4 (w/w) was selected for subsequent studies.
Single-factor experiments

Following the determination of the composition of ATPS, an investigation was conducted to examine the impact of single-factor conditions (including sonication temperature, sonication time, sonication power, particle size, and solid-to-liquid ratio) on the extraction rates of GLA. The results demonstrated a progressive increase in GLA extraction yield with rising temperatures, reaching an optimum at 75  C (Fig. 2C). However, a declining trend in extraction yield was observed as the temperature further increased. This phenomenon aligns with previous research, which suggests that higher extraction temperatures enhance the diffusion and solubility of flavonoids in solvents, although excessively high temperatures may result in flavonoid degradation.. Consequently, the optimal temperature for extraction was determined to be approximately 75  C.

Subsequently, the extraction efficiency of GLA exhibited variability in response to alterations in ultrasonic power and duration. It is well established that ultrasound can damage plant surfaces, thereby promoting the release and dissolution of bioactive compounds (L. B.). The findings demonstrated that the extraction efficiency of GLA reached its pinnacle after 50 min and at an ultrasonic power of 648 W, surpassing the outcomes obtained from lengthier ultrasonic durations and higher power levels (Fig. 2D and E). This phenomenon can be attributed to the degradation of the target compound under prolonged exposure to high-power ultrasonic conditions, leading to a reduction in extraction efficiency. Consequently, the optimal ultrasonic time and power were around 50 min and 648 W, respectively.

Additionally, the present study investigated the impact of particle size and solid-to-liquid ratio on the extraction yield of GLA. Previous research has demonstrated the significance of these factors in extracting compounds from natural products. Our findings indicate that the extraction yields of GLA were maximized when the sample had a particle size of 10 meshes and a solid-to-liquid ratio of 1/50 (Fig. 2F and G). Consequently, the optimal particle size and solid-to-liquid ratio for GLA extraction were approximately 10 meshes and 1/50, respectively.
Optimization of extraction conditions by BBD

RSM has proven to be an effective approach for optimizing extraction processes, offering significant savings in both time and raw materials. To examine the impact of extraction temperature, extraction time, and extraction power on the response variable (Z value), a series of 17 experiments were systematically designed using the BBD. Among them, the selection range of each factor is determined according to the best results of single factor test. In general, the best screening result is selected as the "0" level of RSM, and the low and high levels of response surface optimization are selected on both sides of the best conditions. Table S1 provides a detailed presentation of the RSM independent variables and response variables. The collected data were analyzed through multiple regression analysis, and the resulting model was expressed using a second-order polynomial equation. The equations below represent the second-order polynomial in terms of the coded levels for the responses and variables:

The reliability of the model is illustrated by the results of ANOVA. As shown in Table S2, As shown in Table S2, the significance of the model's p-value (p < 0.0001) indicates that the model is significant for quantification of all responses. At the same time, the lack of fit item p = 66.54 > 0.05 was not significant, which proved that the selection of the model was appropriate. In addition, R2 value is 0.9986, R2Adj value is 0.9968, indicating that the measured value and the predicted value of the results have a good fit. The model can be used to predict and truly reflect the experimental results. C.V.% indicates the accuracy of the test. C.V.% = 0.35 in this experiment indicates that the experimental operation is reliable. Therefore, the model explained the relationship between independent variables and responses sufficiently.
Response surfaces (3D) representations for GLA in licorice.
Fig. 3

To elucidate the interaction between the two factors, it is imperative to ascertain the optimal levels for each experimental variable. Accordingly, response surface plots were generated based on regression model equations. The response surface curve depicted in Fig. 3A-C reveals a peak within the experimental domain, suggesting that the factor ranges are appropriate. Furthermore, it was observed that the extraction yield of GLA increased with extended ultrasonic time, elevated temperature, and enhanced power. However, the extraction yield did not exhibit a continuous increase. The response surface analysis identified the optimal values for the three variables as 51 min, 76  C, and 640 W, respectively, yielding a GLA content of 2040.36 mug/g. Under the predicted optimal conditions, the measured GLA content was 2049.51 mug/g, closely aligning with the predicted value. This outcome demonstrates the efficacy of the established model in optimizing the UA-ATPE process.
